EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:56:01 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Czech public broadcasters hold historic strike following government vote to abolish license fees https://euobserver.com/246573/czech-public-broadcasters-hold-historic-strike-following-government-vote-to-abolish-license-fees/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:56:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246573 Thousand of Czechs joined public TV and radio workers in their walkout over the Czech government's moves to bring public broadcasting under its political control.]]> First published in Deník N.

A strike by workers of public TV and radio workers interrupted broadcasts and drew thousands of people onto the streets across the Czech Republic.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Prague, Brno and Ostrava demonstrations supported by media, students, theatres and more than 300 Czech athletes.

“An unprecedented day in the history of Czech public service media has begun”, said Michal Kubal, Czech Television’s news chief, at 00:00 on 3 November 2026 marking a start to an all-day strike by the broadcasting workers.

He read an opening statement from a sheet of paper during the midnight dispatch. “This broadcast will change. The midnight news is one of many programmes that will look completely different on Czech Television screens from what viewers are used to,” Daniel Stach said on air. The organiser of the strike appeared on TV with a darkened studio as backdrop.

Presenter Kubal went on to explain that staff at Czech Television and Czech Radio were using the one-day strike to fight for independence of both public service media outlets, in response to a government moves to scrap license fees and move public their funding to the state budget.

Read more

Czech government approves first step to scrapping TV and radio licence fees in 4.36am vote, sparking protests

TV management had concluded a memorandum with the strike organisers under which media staff would provide essential news coverage in the event of extraordinary developments.

“A large majority of women and men working at both media outlets have joined the strike. This afternoon, they will also take part in public gatherings in Prague and other cities in support of public service media,” Kubal added.

Those tuning into ČT24 could see a notice about the the public broadcaster’s news network minimalist provisional regime.

“Czech Television employees are on strike. We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue providing a public service in full and to the highest standard in the future,” the notice read.

A STEM/MARK survey for Czech Television says 68 percent of people of Czechs agree public service media should stay well away from state control or private ownership.

“Thank you for watching Czech Television — in times of crisis, at historically pivotal moments and on entirely ordinary weekdays,” said Stach, one of the leading figures of the Veřejnoprávně initiative, which called the strike, as he concluded the roughly five-minute midnight news bulletin.

]]> Firefighters from 19 countries protest EU disaster budget cuts in Brussels https://euobserver.com/246651/firefighters-from-19-countries-protest-eu-disaster-budget-cuts-in-brussels/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:20:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246651 Around 1,000 firefighters from 19 countries gathered in Brussels Tuesday to demand more equipment, more staff, and adequate healthcare, only weeks before key EU budget negotiations.]]> Around 1,000 firefighters from 19 countries gathered in Brussels on Tuesday (3 November) to demand more equipment, more staff, and adequate healthcare, only weeks before key EU budget negotiations.

With wildfires growing bigger and more often due to climate change, there needs to be more professional firefighters, with modern equipment, to face them, argues the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), who organised the protest together with various Belgian workers’ organisations.

As of 7 October, 692 419 hectares burnt in wildfires across the EU this year – an area almost as big as the Greek island of Crete – burning some 30 million tonnes of CO2. Southern countries, Portugal, Greece, Italy, and Spain, suffered most. According to the World Health Organisation, wildfires in Europe have increased by 57 percent since 2022.

Read more

Europe’s summer of wildfires puts spotlight on economic cost of climate inaction

On average, wildfires cause some €2.5bn losses across the EU each year.

The protest gathered in front of a conference on civil protection organised by the EU Commission, where crisis management commissioner Hadja Lahbib presented new guidelines on what citizens should prepare for the first days of an emergency.

The firefighters and unions were there to protest the cuts to the next EU budget for disaster management: from over €10bn requested by the commission to just under €7bn proposed by the Irish presidency last month. Yet that would still be double what the 2021-2027 budget had room for.

“I believe that the risk is getting bigger. So yes, it’s necessary to also increase the support,” Tiago da Cunha, president of a municipality in northern Portugal, where the most summer wildfires hit in 2026, told EUobserver.

Read more

Europe’s 2026 wildfires show the cost of ignoring prevention

Stalo Yostili, 43, has been a firefighter in Cyprus for a decade. She said her country does not recognise how dangerous the profession is. She complained of too few staff, which means for an operation that would normally need 15 firefighters, only six are sent, making it more potentially dangerous.

Profession-specific healthcare is also a big topic, Ireneusz Kierzkowski from the Polish firefighter union, told EUobserver. Retired firefighters often have PTSD, and they also develop cancers more often.

Speaking to EUobserver ahead of the US-mid term elections, taking place on Tuesday (3 November), Gardner says foreign relations are widely under the remit of the executive branch.

“Those who are hoping for a big change from this midterm in terms of US policy. You are probably going to be disappointed,” he said.

With two years left in his presidency, the US-mid terms are largely seen as referendum on the Trump administration; spanning everything from high fuel prices, an unpopular war in Iran, corruption, tariffs, healthcare and immigration.

Trump, in his closing speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, instead largely spoke about algae blooms and paint jobs and other building projects around Washington DC.

“The pipes now are totally renovated,” he said, in reference to botched efforts to renovate the pool.

Democrats need three more seats to take the House and flip four in the Senate without losing any of their own. All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, compared to 35 of 100 in the Senate.

But a Democrat Congress could potentially embolden Trump to push for an even more radical foreign policy, warned Gardner.

“It often happens in the past when presidents lose control of the House and Senate, they pick up the shiny toy that they have, which is foreign policy, because that’s where they have basically very wide discretion,” he said.

“If the Democrats win both, it becomes even more radical,” he added.

]]> Microsoft cloud in Ireland under fire for hosting Israeli app used to monitor Palestinians in occupied West Bank https://euobserver.com/246599/microsoft-cloud-in-ireland-under-fire-for-hosting-israeli-app-used-to-monitor-palestinians-in-occupied-west-bank/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:49:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246599 Microsoft hosts key software used to monitor movements of Palestinians in the occupied West bank. Some of this is being hosted in Ireland. ]]> Microsoft software plays a key part in running an app used by Israel to control Palestinian mobility in the occupied territories, a new report found. 

Al Munasseq, meaning ‘The Coordinator’ in Arabic, is an app launched by Israel’s Coordination of Government Activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (COGAT) unit in 2019 to manage the movement of Palestinians for work, healthcare, prayer, and everyday tasks.

A report published on Tuesday (3 November) by global consumer group Ekō found Microsoft to be hosting key components of Al Munasseq in data centres in Ireland, effectively enabling what is feared to be mass surveillance.

“For Palestinians, Al Munasseq is the gatekeeper to ordinary life. A cancer patient who needs radiotherapy in Jerusalem, a worker who needs to feed his family, a daughter who wants to sit beside her mother in hospital – all of them must ask Israel’s military for a permit to move across their own stolen land, and that permission runs through the Al Munasseq app,” said Ekō senior campaign director, Rewan Al-Haddad.

Read more

EU risks funding Israeli firms which help develop NAZA-type violent tech

“If a Western tech giant can host the machinery powering apartheid in Ireland, inside the EU, and face no consequences, every other company will learn it can do the same,” Al-Haddad told EUobserver. 

Deputy Sinead Gibney, who serves on the Irish parliament’s AI committee, called for an investigation in light of the report findings.

    ]]>         Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government https://euobserver.com/246552/serbias-student-list-has-been-inspirational-but-the-big-test-will-be-forming-a-stable-anti-corruption-government/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:15:05 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246552 The Serbian campaign looked exceptional. I cannot think of many cases of an opposition that was so decentralised and so democratic internally. The closest comparison may be the early German Greens that had a strong Basisdemokratie ["Grassroots Democracy"] out of conviction; or the faceless and fluid democratic movement in Hong Kong ("Be Water") out of necessity. This is inspirational.]]> The ink had hardly dried under articles explaining lessons learned from Péter Magyar’s electoral overthrow of Hungary’s government, when Serbia’s Student List managed to overthrow the semi-authoritarian Aleksandar Vučić.

    Both cases had similarities: long-standing rulers that lied and flaunted their corruption ever more openly; they were ripe for defeat.

    In both cases the opposition avoided strongly partisan positioning and instead focused on state functioning and anti-corruption. 

    Intriguingly, they had almost identical results: 53 percent of the vote for the opposition, 39 percent for the incumbent party. In both cases the opposition showed unity and campaigned across the country and on social media; a well-known ingredient of any campaign to overthrow entrenched authoritarians. 

    Read more

    Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll

    In other ways the two cases are strikingly different.

    The Hungarian campaign was focused on Magyar, a consummate politician and former Fidesz member, who knew the incumbent party from the inside.

    In Serbia a collective of students from different universities turned massive mobilisation against the corrupt government into an electoral platform. 

    In Hungary, Magyar dominated his party, in Serbia, the student collective reached decisions democratically, voting on all major points; an extreme contrast between a one-man show and a movement that hardly had any individual faces. 

    What can we learn from these elections?

    First, we should not get fixated on silver bullets. One success story does not mean that the same recipe works elsewhere. Social movements and electoral campaigns are highly complex and contingent on circumstances. No leader like Magyar appeared in Serbia, no massive student initiative developed in Hungary, although both had similar problems of political repression by the ruling party.

    ]]>         Merz, Meloni and the EU: How political attacks on rescue charities are leaving migrants to drown https://euobserver.com/246480/merz-meloni-and-the-eu-how-political-attacks-on-rescue-charities-are-leaving-migrants-to-drown/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:47:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246480 Berlin, Rome and Brussels have played a role in the decline in an increasingly vital force in the Mediterranean. Search-and-rescue ships have been hampered by legal hurdles and funding cuts, while the central Mediterranean has become a grave for tens of thousands of people.]]> Search-and-rescue NGO efforts to conduct life-saving work in the Mediterranean face continuous derailment by European authorities hoping to stop migrants reaching EU soil – and drowning thousands in the process.

    Since Friedrich Merz took over as German chancellor in May 2025, all funding to national search-and-rescue organisations has stopped. 

    The conservative leader has faced accusations from other EU leaders that the German NGO vessels prevalent across the central Mediterranean’s deadly zone of migrant crossings have acted as a ‘pull factor’, attracting migration to the EU. 

    Current foreign affairs minister Johann Wadephul went so far as to allege that sea rescue organisations are “enabling people-smuggling gangs to carry out their business” in 2023.

    “Of course we know that people don’t travel into the Mediterranean because there are NGOs [there]. They are escaping famine, conflict, violence, some people are even trapped in Libya,” said Sofia [the charity’s workers use first names only], communications coordinator on board German charity SOS Humanity’s mothership.

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    After rescuing 28 people adrift in an overcrowded dinghy last week, the humanitarian NGO has now in total rescued 5,213 people since August 2022. A third of those were children. 

    SOS Humanity were part of a former funding pool that split €2m from Germany’s federal budget for humanitarian aid between search-and-rescue organisations. Despite growing fuel costs, and increasing legal costs from administrative barriers and port detentions by the Italian government, search-and-rescue groups are now dealing with an astronomical gap in their budget. 

    This has also been compounded since Giorgia Meloni’s far-right Italian government came into power in 2022. 

    Rescue charities operating in the central Mediterranean have subsequently been subject to decree 1/2023, requiring them to navigate directly towards the assigned port of safety following a rescue at sea – in other words, preventing more than one rescue operation at a time.

    Italy’s assigned ports are usually days away from where the rescue took place, with the extra navigation due to distant ports causing SOS Humanity to sail an additional 24,745 km and 62 days in 2025 alone. The exacerbated costs of fuel has caused the group to have to severely reduce its operations for 2027.

    Costly ops, and an alarming human cost

    This comes at a time when their work has become more important than ever.

    ]]>         When adults take over youth protests, EU children’s own demands vanish https://euobserver.com/246292/when-adults-take-over-youth-protests-eu-childrens-own-demands-vanish/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:25:18 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246292 As youth protests spread from France to Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece and Albania, Europe is confronting a stark test of whether under‑18s are treated as political actors in their own right, or merely as props in adult power struggles.]]> France’s lycée students have taken to the streets over shortages of teachers, crumbling buildings, and inequalities that determine educational opportunities and university admissions.

    Yet, as political parties and trade unions joined the protests and students found themselves confronted by riot police, the debate shifted from their demands to their inability to act for themselves.

    In France, adultism has deep roots, reflected in negative stereotypes of young people, their gradual exclusion from public spaces, and the persistent assumption that children are politically innocent and therefore easily manipulated by adults.

    Here lies a democratic paradox: children are expected to develop into politically responsible citizens, but when they start behaving like them, their political agency suddenly becomes questionable.

    Lost in this debate, however, is the fact that students are making political claims of their own, challenging not only their school conditions, but also the political decisions and budgetary priorities that perpetuate these inequalities and jeopardise their future.

    Read more

    Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting

    A right to speak, but who will listen?

    Beyond the political controversy, children are already political citizens, even without voting rights.

    The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by every state except the United States, guarantees freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly, and requires children’s views to be given due weight in matters affecting them.

    The EU and France also have legal provisions recognising children’s participation rights, including in educational governance.

    However, political citizenship extends beyond a formal legal status to participation in public life, where children can actively exercise political agency through expression, collective action, and political claims.

    Their exclusion from electoral politics does not diminish their political legitimacy, nor relieve states of their obligation to take their voices seriously.

    But can blockades and protests bring about the change children demand? Faced with  hundreds of thousands of demonstrators taking to the streets across France in support of students, the French government appears to have rediscovered the virtues of listening to children, launching consultations and promising stronger student representation, more teachers, and funding for school renovations.

    Student representatives welcomed some of these commitments, but insisted on seeing actual renovations and additional teachers in classrooms.

    With the 2027 presidential election approaching in France, these commitments risk becoming entangled in campaigning, and potentially overshadowing children’s demands with competing political agendas.

    The question is what will come of the promises; and just as importantly, who will be held accountable, and how, if those promises are never delivered?

    Read more

    Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate

    Adults arrive, children disappear?

    The growing involvement of adults (teachers, parents, unions) in the protests also fuelled accusations of political instrumentalisation: the government was quick to accuse left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) of manipulating the children.

    If there was any adult interference, it deserves scrutiny, but assuming that children must be manipulated whenever they organise politically is mere adultism disguised as paternalistic concern. 

    Concerns over the criminalisation of children’s protests have also grown. While incidents of vandalism and violence overshadowed students’ demands, the crackdown was striking: by 14 October, 6,773 minors had been taken into custody, with 2,190 of them facing prosecution.

    Children are apparently mature enough to face legal consequences, even as their political competence is questioned.

    Meanwhile, investigations into police violence against minors raise questions about the state’s duty to protect them.

    As the riots of 17 October erupted into violence and chaos, students’ demands seemed to have faded from sight amid an increasingly heated debate over public order and wider social and political tensions.

    Meanwhile, protests by young people have also taken place elsewhere in Europe, in Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece, and Albania.

    Although grievances and political circumstances differ, these protests reveal an important distinction between schoolchildren and university students as political citizens.

    Most university students can vote, allowing them to turn collective mobilisation into electoral pressure, as Serbia’s student-backed movement showed when it won the parliamentary election on 25 October.

    But most secondary-school pupils have no equivalent leverage: their political citizenship depends on adults and institutions taking their demands seriously, without constantly calculating how many votes they could win or lose. 

    Beyond the diverse political interpretations of these protests lies another important question: what will children themselves take away from these experiences, and how might these impact their political citizenship?

    They may seek greater influence through consultations, intensify protests or create alternative forms of participation.

    But if their demands continue to fall on deaf ears, while protesting exposes them to the threat of police repression and to adultism, disillusionment may instead drive some away from political participation altogether.

    The promise of children’s rights to be heard was certainly more ambitious than that.

    ]]>         Czech MEP Markéta Gregorová stopped at Chinese border in ‘pseudo-scare tactics’ https://euobserver.com/246452/czech-mep-marketa-gregorova-stopped-at-chinese-border-in-pseudo-scare-tactics/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:04:19 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246452 MEP Markéta Gregorová claims to have been stopped in Beijing in what she called “pseudo-scare tactics” over the arrest of a Chinese national accused of spying in Czech Republic.]]> Czech Pirate MEP Markéta Gregorová (Greens/EFA) claims to have been detained in Beijing for 1.5 hours in what she called “pseudo-scare tactics” over the arrest of a Chinese national accused of spying in the Czech Republic.

    ]]>         Listen: What’s at stake for Europe in the US midterms? https://euobserver.com/246416/listen-whats-at-stake-for-europe-in-the-us-midterms/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:46:54 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246416 Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate and according to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate. According to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.

    What would a Democratic win actually change for Europeans? First, a quick word on what to expect tonight. Polls suggest a win for the Democrats camp, especially in the House of Representatives. 

    It is actually common for the president’s party to lose ground at the midterms. And Donald Trump’s approval ratings have been falling steadily.

    So, if the Democrats do win, what could they do? Quite a lot, on paper at least. Congress holds significant powers. The House can, for instance, launch impeachment proceedings against the president. But removing him from office would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which is very hard to reach.

    The Democrats have said they would open investigations into the administration, including on corruption. They want to keep financial support for Ukraine in place, and to end the war in Iran. They also want to roll back many of the tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

    Read more

    THIS WEEK: EU enlargement report tops Brussels agenda as ‘coalition of the willing’ faces Trump’s midterm test

    These are all issues of great importance for Europe. But could the Democrats really undo them?

    For several of these issues, a simple majority is enough to pass a law. So on that front, they could take a stand. But there is a catch: the president has a veto.

    And to override this veto, Congress needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers. In the House, that means around 290 seats. And even in the most optimistic polls, the Democrats don’t get there.

    Those polls currently point to a tight race for the Senate, and a more comfortable Democratic win in the House.

    Of course, these are estimates to be taken with a pinch of salt. The BBC reminded us yesterday that polls in the United States regularly get it wrong, although they do so less often for midterms.

    Read more

    Trump, Rubio and Hegseth are fumbling Ukraine – Europe needs to stop making the same mistake

    In any case, a two-thirds majority looks like an unlikely scenario. Still, this doesn’t mean nothing will change. The Democrats would still have some levers if they do win.

    They could, for example, block bills by simply refusing to vote for them. And they could hold up the budget, and with it, the funding of the war effort.

    In the case of the tariffs, the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Donald Trump had overstepped his powers since Congress had not approved the tariffs. This is already a difficulty, even if, for now, the government is playing with the legal basis of the tariffs. 

    So, to sum up: the Democrats wouldn’t be able to overturn Donald Trump’s policies altogether, but they could make his life a lot harder.

    ]]>         Andrew Tate’s toxic legacy in Romania is warping its democracy https://euobserver.com/246239/andrew-tates-toxic-legacy-in-romania-is-warping-its-democracy/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:17:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246239 While prosecutors chase the Tates across borders, their macho fantasy of domination is already shaping how a frustrated generation of Romanian men sees women and democracy itself.]]> Prosecutors in Romania officially charged social media influencers Andrew and Christian Tate with trafficking and sex offences involving minors on 4 September. But the Tates were not around to be hauled into a police station in Bucharest – they were in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK on similar charges.

    That two of the world’s most high-profile misogynists may finally be brought to justice is a reason to celebrate. But in the country which hosted them for so many years, their toxic legacy continues to pollute the atmosphere.

    Why did the Tates choose Romania in the first place?

    Before his arrest Andrew Tate expressed a preference for countries where “corruption is accessible to everybody.” 

    An underregulated webcam industry and struggles with combating sex trafficking could also be contributing factors.

    But this only partially explains why the self-styled ‘king of toxic masculinity’ may have based himself here since 2017, and why his poisonous messages had fertile ground in which to germinate.

    Once we understand that, we might be able to start pushing back before it’s too late. 

    Read more

    Why AI-turbocharged misogyny and porn are threats to EU democracy

    Compared to other countries in the region, Romania’s feminist movement is relatively young.

    A fertile ground for toxic masculinity

    In 2000, the Romanian edition of Playboy published a supposedly satirical article titled: “How to Beat Your Wife Without Leaving Marks.”

    The outrage prompted the first major waves of protests and women’s rights activism against gender-based violence and its normalisation in Romanian society.

    But in 2026, Romania ranks low in European rankings on gender equality metrics, and high on incidents of domestic violence.

    Romania has no mandatory gender equality education and no comprehensive sex education, while across swathes of the country, boys and young men lack access to quality education and jobs.

    Successive governments have failed to improve their circumstances, and traditional, social pressure on men to provide for a family or partner fosters anger and resentment.

    The manosphere’s appeal

    This disillusioned generation presents ripe pickings for demagogues like the Tates to sell a cartoonish fantasy of success based on subjugating women. 

    Because of lack of any national data, our organisation helped conduct the first nationally representative study into how rapid social and technological advances are reshaping the values, gender perceptions, and political choices of young Romanian men.

    Our findings show a mixed picture where patriarchal beliefs endure but alongside self-confidence issues over how to bond with women.

    While 53 percent strongly agree that “in a relationship, a woman should be available for sex whenever her partner wants it,” a slightly higher percentage believe that women still do not have adequate rights. 

    The dividing lines are not created by age or urban versus rural but by education and economic precariousness.

    A quarter of respondents with university education agree that a man’s honour must be defended through violence, a figure that rises to 50 percent by those with vocational education.

    Whereas formal education covering these issues is absent, the online environment fills the vacuum and the misogynistic, racist, and homophobic values of the manosphere connect to extreme-right movements in Romania and worldwide.

    Our concerns are that the Tates’ legacy on the minds of young people is so damaging that we may only see the true effects in years to come.

    A better model of masculinity

    But it is never too late to act. In April, Romanian parliament overwhelmingly supported a new law defining the concept of femicide with offenders given potential life sentences.

    The legislation also calls for teaching on gender equality and non-violent relationships to be included in the national curriculum, though this is yet to be implemented.

    Many young men are still open to alternative ideas, so we have time to shape their attitudes and we should not delay – 72 percent interviewed agree democracy is a good form of government but 58 percent want a strong leader who does not bother with parliament or elections. 

    As a riposte to the commercial masculinity bootcamps run by manosphere characters, our organisation runs free and healthy masculinity camps for young men between 18 to 22 years old.

    Led mostly by male trainers, participants from across the country and from a broad socioeconomic background discuss their ideas of masculinity, democracy, extremism, and mental health.

    Many describe loneliness, a lack of physical spaces to build friendships, and a growing guilt for being male.

    Providing young men with a non-judgmental environment to open up is a better way to ensure a safer society, rather than putting the onus on women to change their behaviour. 

    Young men also need to be taught media literacy, so they can recognise hate speech and radicalisation techniques used by the manosphere and the far right to target them.

    Positive male role models can encourage young men to open up about problems, but they also need to be exposed to narratives instilling the values of democracy and pluralism.

    Online platforms remain vastly under-regulated, while offline spaces that provide young people, male and female, with environments in which to socialise and form meaningful connections are lacking. 

    Politicians have successfully harvested the Tates’ audience through skilled social-media targeting, and this bore fruit in the last presidential elections, where young men voted heavily for parties headed by authoritarian leaders.

    The radical right is currently leading the polls, and ongoing political deadlock may yet result in them entering government.

    Young Romanian men are not yet a lost cause, but without a concerted societal effort to combat the sinister forces that influence them, democracy in Romania, and across Europe, may not survive their loss.

    In testimony published in July by the United Nations and the Ukrainian rights group Projector, the woman, identified by the pseudonym Olena, described being dragged away, beaten, and threatened with sexual violence. Her captors demanded the names of other LGBTI people in the city. At the time of publication, she had not reported any of this to Ukrainian law enforcement.

    On 12 October, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky signed a national human rights strategy that, for the first time, devoted a section of its own to LGBTI rights. It identifies LGBTI people as a group at heightened risk and commits the state to fighting discrimination and hate crimes. The strategy is tied to Ukraine’s bid to join the European Union. The cabinet has six months to draw up an implementation plan.

    Read more

    Attacks on LGBTI people are the warning sign of a wider backlash against democracy

    I have watched my country make promises like this before. The decree replaces a strategy that Zelensky signed in 2021. The hate crimes bill introduced that year never reached a vote and was withdrawn in 2025. I want to know what will make this promise any different.

    Parliament acted on another question of minority rights that same day. Hungary had blocked two clusters of Ukraine’s accession talks until Kyiv expanded schooling in EU languages for national minorities.

    Those minorities deserve protection. What struck me was how quickly Parliament could provide it. The bill was introduced at the start of October, passed and signed on 12 October. The next day, the EU opened the two clusters.

    Meanwhile, progress on LGBTI rights has been much slower, despite the EU’s equality benchmarks.

    A registered-partnerships bill for same-sex and different-sex couples, introduced in March 2023, has sat in the legal policy committee ever since.

    A bill adding sexual orientation and gender identity to the criminal code’s hate crime provisions has been in committee since August 2025.

    And Ukraine’s own EU roadmap, adopted in May 2025, set the third quarter of that year as the target for passing partnership legislation – the deadline came and went without a vote.

    In February, the Supreme Court let stand a ruling recognising two men as a family, rejecting a challenge from a conservative campaign group. Two months later, Parliament voted 254 to 2 to advance a new Civil Code reserving, de facto, family unions to a man and a woman.

    Rights groups warn that the wording could prevent similar rulings. The speaker has since submitted amendments restoring the current definition of family. Parliament has yet to vote on them.

    When hate crimes become hooliganism

    These failures matter when someone goes to the police to report an attack. In May, after a rally in Ivano-Frankivsk against the Civil Code, men from a “traditional values” counter-event followed the LGBTI activist Olena Shevchenko and a colleague, knocked them down, and stole their posters.

    The police say officers intervened at once and cited two men for petty hooliganism. The women say they spent hours at the station, where officers tried to discourage them from filing and would not record a discriminatory motive.

    In July, someone left severed pigs’ heads and entrails outside a Kyiv branch of a salon chain that had publicly backed LGBTI rights, and poured blood on the steps. The police opened a case for hooliganism.

    Calling an attack hooliganism can leave out why the victim was targeted. The criminal code does not explicitly list sexual orientation or gender identity as hate crime grounds.

    The European Commission also found last year that Ukraine did not systematically collect data on such crimes. In the first half of 2026, Nash Svit, a Ukrainian rights group, documented violations by police in 10 of the 16 cases involving police that it monitored. In one, a gay man in Lviv reported blackmail and threats to out him.

    Police declined to open a case, saying the matter was too small.

    It is Olena’s decision whether to report what happened to her in Kherson. The state owes her a safe way to do so. Its new strategy acknowledges that distrust of public authorities and fear of stigma keep LGBTI people from seeking help. The government is describing people who fear the very institutions they should be able to turn to.

    A strategy without legal recognition

    The strategy also leaves out a specific commitment to legally recognise same-sex partnerships, as the National LGBTI Consortium has pointed out.

    A 2023 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights found the lack of recognition discriminatory. Ukraine is bound by that judgment as a party to the European Convention on Human Rights, and whether or not it joins the EU, accession talks add leverage and a timetable, and Ukraine has already missed the deadline in its own roadmap.

    Read more

    [Interview] Ukrainian MP Ivanna Klympush: ‘I would like to see the countries that joined the EU and had no problems with corruption’

    In July, I wrote in The New York Times about LGBTI soldiers waiting for the state to recognise their partners. Olena was a shop assistant who kept a flag. Nobody should have to become a hero to receive ordinary rights.

    Both bills should go to a vote before the Civil Code’s second reading. The government should fund confidential legal aid outside the big cities and publish how LGBTI complaints are handled, with identities protected. The EU should hold Ukraine to the benchmark it has already written, which names the 2023 judgment.

Ukraine cannot undo what Russian soldiers did to her in Kherson, but it can make sure that, if she ever walks into a police station, she gets protection and her complaint is taken seriously.     EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    The COP17 biodiversity summit wrapped up on Saturday morning in Yerevan. Delegates from nearly every country were in the room, yet very little came out of it.

    So what should we take away from it? Let’s start with the problem that comes up at almost every COP.

    They bring together a huge number of countries. And they all need to back the declaration at the end. So it is very hard to agree on measures that actually have an impact.

    There was one success, though, back in 2022. Participants adopted the Kunming-Montreal framework, with clear targets: restoring at least 30 percent of degraded ecosystems by 2030, and providing 20 billion dollars a year in financial aid to developing countries.

    That was four years ago. So are these goals on track? No. Several reports published ahead of the COP sounded the alarm.

    Read more

    No extra funds for biodiversity at UN meeting, as vast majority of EU natural treasures left unprotected

    According to one of them, and this is staggering, not a single target is on track.
    To reach the global goals, investment in ecosystem restoration would need to be multiplied by four.

    It’s a bit like the climate COPs, with their limited results since the famous Paris Agreement in 2015. Except that biodiversity gets even less media attention, and therefore even less pressure to deliver.

    That said, let’s not throw the baby out with the bathwater. The commitments are often disappointing compared with what is needed. But they are still better than nothing.

    So what did countries actually agree on? First, they agreed on the diagnosis I just mentioned: that countries are behind on their 2030 goals. That alone was already a fight.

    Then there is a call to speed up work, but in very broad terms. Language never goes far, because every single country has to sign off. And that, of course, is the heart of the problem.

    On the two most anticipated topics, there was no real breakthrough. The first is subsidies that contribute to destroying nature. We’re talking, for example, about subsidies for fossil fuels or pesticide production.

    According to a report by the International Institute for Sustainable Development, governments spend no less than 2 trillion dollars on them every year.

    Read more

    Europe can’t lead on nature at COP17 while cutting biodiversity cash at home

    But the talks led to very little. That’s because several countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, India, and even Brazil, held back ambition.

    To the point that the adopted texts don’t even name these harmful subsidies. All they say is that parties are encouraged to work towards Target 18 of the Kunming-Montreal framework. Which, in the end, will only mean something to those who know the framework inside out.

    The second topic met more or less the same fate: this was about funding for developing countries. Basically, everyone agrees that more financial aid is needed, but nobody wants to commit to giving more. The only concrete commitment is to take stock, by next year, of what each country is really contributing.

    Now, despite those poor results, most of the NGOs present in Yerevan still defend the COP process. As I said, it’s better than nothing.

    For example, one outcome was a decision recognising the work of IPBES, the biodiversity equivalent of the IPCC.

    Even that was a battle for nature’s defenders. But recognising the facts and the science is the starting point for everything else. So we should not throw that away.

      <description><p>Affordability and small businesses’ economic woes feature heavily in the House race for Wisconsin’s third district</p><p>After 18 years in business, Erin Klaus is closing her storefront, a handmade artisan market in downtown Eau Claire, Wisconsin, at the end of the year.</p><p>She opened Tangled Up in Hue amid a recession, during a time when downtown was “kind of a ghost town”, weathering construction and the pandemic.       <title>The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 03 Nov 2026 19:02:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Charlie Chawke’s pub company returns to profit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/charlie-chawke-pub-company-returns-to-profit/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/charlie-chawke-pub-company-returns-to-profit/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:30:48 +0000The company that operates three of Charlie Chawke’s pubs, including Ireland’s most expensive pub, The Old Orchard in Rathfarnham, returned to profit last year with pretax profits of €1.03 million. The pub was bought by Chawke in 2005 for a record €22 million.

Accounts filed by Milltown Inns and subsidiaries for the Old Orchard and the Dropping Well pubs in Dublin and Aunty Lena’s bar in Adare, Co Limerick show it recorded the pretax profits as revenues dipped by 2 per cent from €11.13 million to €10.94 million in the 12 months to the end of October 2025.

A note with the accounts from the directors said that “during the financial year, the group encountered several challenges that impacted overall profitability”.

The note said that while the underlying business operations remained resilient, supported by steady revenue growth across key segments, “profitability was significantly affected by increased interest expenses”.

The accounts said that the group’s EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) for the year amounted to €1.42 million “representing a solid level of earnings relative to turnover, despite a decrease in turnover compared to the prior year”.

Along with operating the pubs, the group also owns a number of investment properties.

The pretax profit of €1.03 million last year followed a pretax loss of €5.95 million for 2024 which was due to a non-cash write-down of €6.2 million in the value of its freehold investment property.

In 2025, the group also benefited from ‘other income’ totalling €295,990 which included rental income of €204,490.

The group’s profits were also boosted by booking a €610,678 increase in the value of investment property in 2025. It recorded a post tax profit of €923,343 after incurring a corporation tax charge of €114,406.

The accounts show that interest on loans decreased sharply from €767,183 to €611,726.

The interest costs are mainly connected to the Old Orchard purchase in 2005.

The profits last year take account of combined non-cash depreciation and amortisation costs of €375,428.

The group successfully refinanced its banking arrangements by entering into a new financing facility in February 2025. A note states that “this new facility replaces the existing borrowing arrangement and provides extended credit terms”.

The group’s net debt reduced from €14.36 million to €11.53 million.

Numbers employed decreased from 176 to 167 made up of 159 in “bar and restaurant”, six in administration and two in management.

Staff costs totalled €4.27 million.

Shareholder funds at the end of October 2025 totalled €2.77 million.

]]><![CDATA[Regulator last year recommended that Government should give RTÉ additional €35m in 2027]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/regulator-last-year-recommended-that-government-should-give-rte-additional-35m-in-2027/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/regulator-last-year-recommended-that-government-should-give-rte-additional-35m-in-2027/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:34:57 +0000Ireland’s media regulator recommended that the Government allocate an additional €35 million in funding to RTÉ in 2027, almost double the shortfall that was a source of controversy in last month’s budget.

Coimisiún na Meán (CnaM) recommended that the broadcaster receive a total of €275 million next year to help it hit its voluntary redundancy scheme targets and achieve its goal of commissioning more programming from independent producers.

RTÉ was allocated €240 million in the budget last month, €20 million lower than what was agreed as part of a landmark multiyear deal, unexpectedly freezing its funding at 2026 levels. Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan said at the time that he was displeased with the pace of reform at the broadcaster, specifically its voluntary exit scheme through which it is targeting some 400 job cuts.

Executives from the broadcaster, including director general Kevin Bakhurst, will appear before the Oireachtas Media Committee on Wednesday to discuss reform at the organisation and issues around funding.

In advance of the meeting, RTÉ sent a briefing document to committee members.

The document, seen by The Irish Times, reveals that CnaM recommended that the Government allocate an additional €15 million to RTÉ in 2026 and again in 2027 relative to what it was supposed to receive under the multiyear funding agreement reached with the previous Coalition in 2024.

RTÉ likely to get back €20m lost in Budget 2027 ‘if it proves reforms are on track’

It would mean that the broadcaster would receive €255 million instead of €240 million this year, and €275 million instead of €260 million in 2027.

The regulator made its recommendations in its most recent five-year review of public funding for public service media, which was published and sent to O’Donovan in the summer of 2025.

The recommendations “reflected CnaM’s statutory responsibilities, strategic objectives, regulatory experience and broad evidence base gathered through research and consultation”, RTÉ has told committee members in advance of the meeting.

CnaM also sent a separate annual funding review to the minister earlier this year, details of which have not yet been published.

In its most recent annual review sent to the minister in July 2025, the regulator and consultancy firm Oliver & Ohlbaum Associates warned that RTÉ’s €240 million allocation for 2026 was “insufficient to fully support RTÉ’s sustainability, strategy and delivery of public service objectives”.

The decision to allocate €240 million again in 2027 sparked a political row after the budget last month.

O’Donovan warned Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers in a letter before the budget that the Coalition would “renege” on its funding deal with RTÉ if more cash was not found for his department.

In the final reckoning, an additional €21 million was allocated to O’Donovan’s department after the letter.

However, RTÉ’s allocation remained the same as in 2026 at €240 million.

Initially expressing shock and dismay at the interdepartmental dispute over RTÉ’s funding allocation, Bakhurst said last week that he is confident the shortfall will be secured.

Meanwhile, in a separate letter sent to the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee last week, RTÉ confirmed that its multiyear funding agreement was formalised in a short email from then-media minister Catherine Martin in 2024.

]]>Colin Keegan<![CDATA[European stocks slip as Middle East uncertainty makes for caution]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/european-stocks-slip-as-middle-east-uncertainty-makes-for-caution/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/european-stocks-slip-as-middle-east-uncertainty-makes-for-caution/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:33:53 +0000Europe’s benchmark equities index slipped on Tuesday, as doubts over a potential Middle East peace deal kept markets ​on edge in advance of the US midterm elections, while investors also assessed a slew of earnings.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index closed 0.58 per cent lower at 645 points, with mining shares leading declines on weaker copper prices.

Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their ​war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. Overnight, the United States carried out what it called defensive strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island.

Brent crude swung between gains and losses and was last ⁠down 1.2 per cent, but above $100 (€88.31) a barrel.

DUBLIN

With oil prices remaining elevated, Ryanair fell almost 1 per cent. The airline has warned that higher fuel prices will soon translate into higher fares.

Cairn Homes rose 1 per cent after the company said Ireland had “little chance” of scaling up home completions to 60,000 a year unless half of all units built are apartments.

Bank of Ireland was down nearly 2 per cent as the outlook for inflation seemed to worsen, increasing the odds of another ECB rate rise next month. The other big mover was food company Glanbia, which saw its shares fall nearly 3 per cent to €19.71.

EUROPE

In Europe, however, Gilles Guibout, head of European equities at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said valuations had cooled, but earnings dynamics were still positive.

“We would rather be in ‘buy on weakness’ mode for the time being, because we don’t think that those investments will be questioned. We could have some projects that could be delayed but, by and large, what we are seeing is that all the investments are fuelled by the need for more ‌compute.”

On the earnings ​front, the German online fashion retailer Zalando fell 6.6 per cent, the ​biggest faller on the Stoxx index, after weaker gross margin and net loss outweighed slightly-better-than-expected sales.

The ‌technology sector lost nearly 1 per cent, with AI heavyweight ​ASML declining 1.6 per cent.

The German pharmaceuticals and agriculture group Bayer rose 3.6 per cent after raising its 2026 ‌profit forecast.

Lufthansa gained 3.9 per cent as analysts pointed to broadly resilient results, despite the carrier trimming its annual profit forecast.

Philips gained 4.8 per cent after reaching a ​preliminary agreement with the US Department of Justice to end investigations linked to the ​Dutch company’s 2021 global recall of sleep and respiratory-care devices.

Sportswear maker Adidas dropped 2.8 per cent after brokerage UBS downgraded it to “sell” from “neutral”.

LONDON

Britain’s FTSE 100 registered its steepest one-day ‌drop in a month on Tuesday, pressured by miners and bank shares, in advance of US midterm elections ‌and this week’s Bank of England interest rate decision.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index ended down 1.1 per cent at 10,638.43 points, ​following four straight sessions of gains. The midcap FTSE 250 index closed 0.5 per cent lower at 24,674.

The FTSE ​350 basic resources index dropped 2.6 per cent, with Antofagasta down 3.5 per cent and Glencore off 2.8 per cent.

Coca-Cola Europacific Partners fell 2.1 per cent after the ‌bottler flagged cost pressures

Primark owner Associated British Foods led the fallers on the FTSE 100 with ​a 2.2 per cent slip after forecasting lower annual profit.

NEW YORK

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq rose on Tuesday as tech stocks ‌found their footing in advance of US midterm election results, though Apple joined the list of Big Tech companies whose earnings failed to impress investors.

Apple fell 2.2 per cent after the iPhone ​maker warned the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring its holiday-quarter gross margin.

Chip stocks were among top gainers, with Nvidia climbing 3 per cent after falling for the last four sessions.

The Nasdaq-100 closed more than 10 per cent below its all-time closing high ​on Monday, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction as investors grow wary of Big Tech’s soaring AI spending and little evidence of adequate returns.

– Additional reporting: Reuters

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[Penneys owner ABF forecasts further profit decline as fast-fashion sales slow]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/penneys-owner-abf-forecasts-further-profit-decline-as-fast-fashion-sales-slow/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/penneys-owner-abf-forecasts-further-profit-decline-as-fast-fashion-sales-slow/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:31:52 +0000Associated British Foods (ABF) has slashed profit guidance for its struggling sugar business and reported declining sales at fast-fashion chain Primark, as the FTSE 100 conglomerate battles challenging conditions on multiple fronts in advance of a planned demerger next year. Primark trades as Penneys in Ireland.

The group said the “duration and severity of the Middle East conflict” had left it expecting to pay higher gas prices in its sugar business next year, while sugar prices in Europe remain at low levels.

High gas prices following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year pushed up refining costs for ABF. Chief executive George Weston said the company was expecting to pay 75 pence (€0.90) per therm for gas next year but now expects to pay £1.05 (€1.25).

As a result, ABF now expects its sugar division to report an operating loss of up to £60 million in 2026, compared to prior expectations for a £25 million loss. ABF’s shares fell by about 2 per cent on Wednesday morning.

The British grocery and retail group is preparing to separate Primark from its food business in a bid to remove a perceived conglomerate discount afflicting ABF, which sells everything from tea bags to animal feed.

Primark’s uneven growth underscores case for ABF split

However, Primark is contending with subdued consumer demand, particularly in continental Europe. Sales at the discount chain fell 2.2 per cent on a like-for-like basis in the third quarter, slightly better than analysts expected, with sales in Europe dropping 3.6 per cent.

The company reiterated its expectation that Primark will report a full-year operating profit margin of approximately 10 per cent.

Sugar sales fell 4 per cent in the third quarter to £451 million, driven mainly by falling demand in Europe, where increasingly health-conscious consumers are cutting back. Sales were also hit by rain-related production delays at its new factory in Tanzania.

Weston said he expected an improvement in the business as European sugar beet producers have been reducing their output in a bid to rebalance supply and demand.

Barclays said the sugar downgrades were “tough to digest”. “Unfortunately, this distracts from a decent Primark result,” said analyst Matthew Clements.

Group sales were flat at £5.3 billion in the quarter. ABF reiterated its expectation that full-year operating profit and earnings per share would decline at a group level.

ABF announced in April that it would separate Primark by the end of 2027 in what is anticipated to be one of the largest-ever FTSE 100 demergers.

]]>Nick Bradshaw for The Irish Times<![CDATA[Ireland unlikely to build 60,000 homes a year without surge in apartments, Cairn warns]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/ireland-unlikely-to-build-60000-homes-a-year-without-surge-in-apartments-cairn-warns/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/ireland-unlikely-to-build-60000-homes-a-year-without-surge-in-apartments-cairn-warns/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:58:17 +0000Ireland has “little chance” of scaling up annual home completions up to 60,000 unless half of all units built each year are apartments, which developers face significant challenges to deliver, one of Ireland’s biggest home builders has said.

Last year, the Government’s new housing plan set a goal of 300,000 home completions by the end of 2030 to address the housing crisis. Meeting this target would require completions to rise from 36,284 last year to 50,000 to 60,000 annually.

A submission by Cairn Homes to the Oireachtas housing committee has forecast close to 40,000 new homes will be built this year and completions in 2027 are “likely to further exceed that number”.

The developer’s chief executive, Michael Stanley, said in a statement to the committee that the building sector’s ability to grow annual completions to meet required demand could be hampered by national housing policy set by the Government.

Stanley said the National Planning Framework (NPF), which has set the strategic direction where and what type of development takes place, mean the State can only deliver around 25,000 to 30,000 own-door houses a year, which means the remainder will need to be apartments.

He added 85 per cent of zoned land has a density requirement that “necessitates some or all apartments within future developments”.

“There is also an important climate and infrastructure rationale behind this approach. The 2023 Climate Action Plan includes a target to reduce total vehicle-kilometres driven by 20 per cent by 2030.”

Last year, 12,047 of the 36,284 homes built were apartments, with 18,308 houses in new-build estates and the remaining 5,929 being one-off homes.

“The biggest resulting change in housing output will be the requirement to massively increase large-scale apartment output to meet land use stipulations,” Stanley said.

Corporate landlord says Ireland's housing shortage has led to profit surge

“Approximately 50 per cent of all new homes in the future will have to be apartments to comply with the objectives of the NPF. This means that unless the industry builds circa 25,000 to 30,000 apartments per year, there is little chance of achieving a total output of 50,000 to 60,000 homes per year.”

Research commissioned by the Department of Housing showed development costs for urban apartments in Dublin rose by more than €13,000 to €605,000 last year, while the price of a suburban apartment rose by 2 per cent to €559,000.

Developers have said the prices required to deliver apartments, and the lack of a viable exit from selling to individual owners or investors, has made many apartment projects unviable to build.

Stanley said the difficultly the industry faces making apartment schemes viable to build could impact the sector’s ability to scale home building up to the rate required to meet the 300,000 goal.

“With apartments forming part of the delivery sequence, a lack of a funding or viable exit for those apartments will have the knock-on effect of restricting or slowing down the delivery of houses and the wider development,” he said.

He added that the sector needs support from the State to make apartment delivery viable “while private capital remains more limited for this category of residential development”.

Opinion: Minister’s refusal to answer questions on house prices reveals confused state of housing policy

The State has set up the Croí Cónaithe (Cities) scheme, which was launched in 2022 to bridge the gap between how much it costs developers to build an apartment and the price owner-occupiers can afford to pay for apartments.

Cairn has sold more than 350 apartments that were built in its new Seven Mills development in Dublin 22 through this scheme at prices between €235,000 and €275,000 for one-bedroom units, while a 79.9sq m two-bedroom apartment costs about €375,000.

]]><![CDATA[Fish-and-chips chain Beshoffs gave EU staff better pay and hours, permit worker claims]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/fish-and-chips-chain-beshoffs-gave-eu-staff-better-pay-and-hours-permit-worker-claims/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/fish-and-chips-chain-beshoffs-gave-eu-staff-better-pay-and-hours-permit-worker-claims/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:21:10 +0000A Turkish worker has said she was discriminated against and made to feel like “rubbish” when her bosses at the Beshoffs fish-and-chips chain refused the annual leave she sought for her own wedding.

The employee, Zerha Fidan, has accused Beshoff Brothers’s operating company Glendalon Ltd of giving European Union nationals better pay, preferential shift allocations and priority for annual leave, in breach of the Employment Equality Act 1998.

She told the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) she could not quit her job as a counter assistant at its restaurant in Clontarf, Dublin 3, even after being denied leave for the wedding, because her residency entitlements in Ireland were tied to her employment.

Her lawyers argue she was discriminated against on the grounds of race, in breach of the Employment Equality Act – a claim being disputed by the restaurant group at the WRC.

Fidan started work at Beshoffs in November 2022, shortly after arriving in Ireland, and worked at various locations before being deployed at its Clontarf restaurant, she told the WRC last week.

Fidan’s evidence was that when the national minimum wage was raised to €12.70 at the start of 2024, she was kept on this rate until August that year, despite two colleagues – both EU nationals – at the shop getting a higher hourly rate.

She said the higher hourly pay for the other two workers was “hidden from me” and only disclosed “accidentally” by one of the women.

The business’s position was that one of the other workers was a supervisor, while the other performed the duties of a supervisor. However, Fidan said both were doing the same job as she was.

Fidan said she approached her manager in November 2024 after becoming engaged and asked for time off in September the following year. His response then, she said, was “Oh, you didn’t invite me.”

She wrote to her manager in February 2025 seeking four weeks off that September – a fortnight as annual leave and a fortnight as unpaid leave, she said.

There was no answer from the manager at that point, and she then wrote to the business’s general manager, Bridget Starbuck, asking about leave for September that year, she said.

Asked how she felt when Starbuck gave no reply, she said: “Rubbish. Who am I, of course?”

She said that having sought a day off for the sixth anniversary of her father’s death in March 2025, the roster was set so that she was required to work for 10 days straight.

This, she said, was “a punishment” for “talking about my salary, my wedding, and I wanted one Saturday off – you know, I am asking every day, every time”.

She said that after the 10-day run of shifts, she suffered a panic attack at work.

Fidan’s doctor placed her on medical leave after that, and suggested in June 2025 that the complainant could go back to work if there were reduced hours, flexibility on start and finish times, and a “calm” working environment, the hearing was told.

Starbuck had replied to the medical letter saying the business could not accommodate Fidan’s return to work on that basis “due to the nature of the role”.

The hearing was told a complaint was filed with the WRC after that.

The case stands adjourned and is not expected to resume before the new year.

]]>chang chang<![CDATA[Lotto regulator receives fewer than 30 complaints in 2025, one over the term ‘easy money’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/lotto-regulator-receives-fewer-than-30-complaints-in-2025-one-over-the-term-easy-money/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/lotto-regulator-receives-fewer-than-30-complaints-in-2025-one-over-the-term-easy-money/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:51:57 +0000The Regulator of the National Lottery received fewer than 30 complaints last year, with the lotto’s online experience listed as the most common issue, although a gripe over the phrase “easy money” has prompted a change of script in its most-viewed gameshow.

Of the 28 complaints submitted to the regulator’s office, 10 were related to online experience, seven were a result of the game’s design, five had to do with the information provided to players and another five were a complaint of the retailer. Only one was regarded as not related to the lottery at all, according to the regulator’s annual report.

However, following two complaints made in 2024 and 2025, the regulator said it requested the removal of expressions such as “easy money” and “giving away lots of cash” from the Telly Bingo programme’s script, which the lottery operator “promptly agreed to”.

“The regulator was concerned that using such terms could be misleading and trivialise the nature of the product,” the organisation wrote in its annual report, as money “is not given away for free or to everyone participating”, but instead is awarded through a random draw to participants who purchased a €2.50 Telly Bingo ticket.

It also reviewed its marketing emails to Lotto account holders, which it sends only when players “have explicitly opted-in to receiving them”. The lotto operator “monitors player activity for risk indicators that are suggestive of problem gambling”, the regulator’s annual report read, and sends a “responsible play communication” to encourage them “to reflect on their spend”.

Online controls may be implemented, such as spending limits, self-exclusion and third-party support services. “Ultimately, this interaction can be escalated to a phone call and, where needed, the exclusion of a player”, the regulator wrote.

It conducted a further review into its marketing practices, finding “the operator routinely disabled marketing emails where certain problem gambling risk indicators were detected”. It further recommended “that marketing emails be disabled for longer periods for this group of players”, which the operator agreed to.

The National Lottery donated nearly €240 million to its “good causes” programme in support of community initiatives, charities and public services, representing a one per cent increase from the previous year.

Sales of national lottery tickets amounted to €871 million last year, up 1.8 per cent from €855 million in 2024, with sales conducted online representing nearly one in five purchases and totalling €155 million.

In the regulator’s financial accounts for the 2025 financial year, the organisation accrued €1.82 million in income and €1.61 million in administrative costs, leaving it with a €210,00 in operating surplus and €3.53 million in retained earnings at the end of the year.

]]><![CDATA[Judge urges Glenman firm brothers to redouble mediation efforts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/03/judge-urges-glenman-firm-brothers-to-redouble-mediation-efforts/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/03/judge-urges-glenman-firm-brothers-to-redouble-mediation-efforts/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:36:45 +0000A judge has urged two brothers at the centre of a High Court row over the running of the Glenman Corporation building firm to “redouble their efforts” to mediate the dispute.

Micheál and Albert Conneally are the sole directors of Glenman which has been involved in the leisure, housing and school building sectors for many years.

Last week, the High Court heard Albert had tried to appoint a third director without his brother’s approval. As a result, Micheál sought and obtained an interim injunction restraining the appointment pending determination of the matter by the court.

This happened, Micheál said, just five weeks before a separate case he is taking alleging shareholder oppression by Albert.

On Tuesday, when the case returned before Judge Brian Cregan, the court was told Albert had filed a replying affidavit to Micheál’s claims.

Albert’s barrister, Martin Hayden, said it may be that the parties come to a realistic resolution over this latest dispute. What his side suggested was that Micheál would meet with this proposed third director.

The third director is independent and a professional contract manager, counsel said. There were two major issues coming to a head in the company and if something is not done about it, substantial damages could be awarded against the company, he said.

His side suggested Micheál meet the proposed third director so he could see if he “liked the cut of his jib” but there had been no response, Hayden said.

Gary McCarthy, counsel for Micheál, said he wanted an opportunity to look at the affidavit filed by Albert.

The judge said the reality of getting a hearing date in relation to the injunction, before December 1st when the oppression case is due to begin, was very slim.

He said this was clearly a very bitter dispute between two brothers and he noted previous mediation efforts did not succeed. Hayden pointed out that he was not involved in that and he was part of a “changing team”.

The judge said he would adjourn the matter for two weeks but he wanted to really encourage the parties to redouble their efforts to mediate. If the case goes to trial it could be bogged down for years in the legal system and that will incur substantial costs, he said.

McCarthy said there had been enormous costs already.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Brussels sets tight deadline for ECB president nominations]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/brussels-sets-tight-deadline-for-ecb-president-nominations/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/brussels-sets-tight-deadline-for-ecb-president-nominations/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:08:19 +0000Brussels has given euro zone governments just days to nominate candidates to become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB), signalling that the race to find Christine Lagarde’s successor could come to a head quickly.

Kyriakos Pierrakakis, president of the Eurogroup and Greek finance minister, has called on the bloc’s 21 member states to submit their nominations by Friday, a spokesperson for the body co-ordinating Eurozone policy said on Tuesday.

Lagarde announced last week that she will step down as ECB president on February 7th, nine months before the end of her eight-year term.

Central Bank of Ireland governor Gabriel Makhlouf said he believes ECB chief economist Philip Lane would be a “great” candidate to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the ECB.

“I think Philip would be great but I don’t know whether legally doing a further term on the executive board is possible,” he said.

Lane’s eight-year term as chief economist expires in May.

Could Ireland’s Philip Lane be in the running for top ECB post?

The change in leadership at Europe’s most powerful monetary authority comes as the region is in the throes of another wave of inflation and growing investor concern over the state of France’s public finances and political stability in the run-up to its presidential elections in April.

Lagarde said last week that she wanted “greater freedom to express her views” on matters other than monetary policy. She has also been in talks with the World Economic Forum over becoming its next chair.

The ECB president and the five other members of its executive board are appointed by the leaders of the 21 countries that use the euro, after consulting with the European parliament and the ECB. A successful candidate needs the support of at least 16 countries representing 65 per cent of the euro area’s population.

EU leaders, who will meet twice this month and again in December, are expected to make a decision before the end of the year on both Lagarde’s replacement and two other seats on the executive board that will also become vacant in 2027.

ECB executive board member Isabel Schnabel will leave to join the IMF in January.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, and Klaas Knot, the former Dutch central bank governor, are seen as the frontrunners to become the fifth ECB president from February. Both are backed by their respective governments.

Hernández de Cos is viewed as a more dovish economist while Knot has a hawkish reputation. However, people familiar with their views stress that both are pragmatists who are keen to forge consensus among policymakers and are not wedded to ideological positions.

After Germany last month signalled that it would not seek the ECB presidency, the odds on a surprise outside candidate to replace Lagarde widened.

However, observers warn that new names could still emerge at the eleventh hour, pointing to the unexpected last-minute nomination of Lagarde by French President Emmanuel Macron in 2019.

According to people familiar with the discussions in various capitals, France is eyeing the ECB chief economist role, which is widely seen as the second most important one after the president. - Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026
