]]>SDI Productions<![CDATA[How can my son find out if his father has cut him out of his will?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000My son’s father and I never married. He has never paid maintenance for him. A few years ago there was a disagreement between them and unfortunately his father hasn’t had any contact with him for about five years.

My ex also has another son who he is very close to. Recently my ex came into some money from the sale of his own father’s house. In the event that he dies, how can our son find out if he left a will?

CC

In an ideal world, we all take care of family, not least when we die, assuming we have the resources to do so. The real world is more messy.

You don’t say whether your former partner was ever a part of your son’s life but he certainly never paid anything to the cost of raising him.

Now middle-aged, your son and his father no longer talk. Meanwhile, his father has a son from a separate relationship to whom he is close, and the father has come into money.

That certainly raises the potential for a dispute when he dies.

There are two scenarios here – one where he has a will and one where he does not. Let’s take them in reverse order.

If there is no will, his estate would be divided according to the Succession Act.

You do not say whether the father ever married – either to the mother of his other son or someone else. If he did, and presuming that spouse survives him, she will receive two-thirds of his estate with his children sharing the final third.

That would include your son, this favoured other son and any other children he might have.

If the spouse does not survive him, or there never was any spouse, the children split the value of the estate between them without regard to favourites. Everything is split evenly.

Whomever applies for the grant of administration intestate is obliged to track down all qualifying beneficiaries – which includes all children regardless of whether they were born inside or outside a marriage. In practice, whomever applies to manage the estate will engage a solicitor as intestacy can be a minefield.

But what if there is a will?

If it is like most other Irish wills and there is a spouse, it will simply leave everything to the spouse. If he does not, the spouse is entitled to what is called a legal right share – which, where there are children, amounts to one-third of the estate.

Assuming any legal right share is respected, the will could make provision for one or other or both sons – and any other children – but it doesn’t have to. There is no obligation for a person to provide in death for adult children or any other relative apart from a spouse.

However, if a child feels that they should be entitled to something in a will, they can take what is called a section 117 action.

Section 117 (1) of the Succession Act 1965 says: “Where, on application by or on behalf of a child of a testator, the court is of opinion that the testator has failed in his moral duty to make proper provision for the child in accordance with his means, whether by his will or otherwise, the court may order that such provision shall be made for the child out of the estate as the court thinks just.”

This is a very wide and nebulous position, with the court taking into account the circumstances of the applicant vis-à-vis other family members among other things.

It clarifies in section 117 (2): “The court shall consider the application from the point of view of a prudent and just parent, taking into account the position of each of the children of the testator and any other circumstances which the court may consider of assistance in arriving at a decision that will be as fair as possible to the child to whom the application relates and to the other children.”

The key thing is that any section 117 application must be made to the court within six months of a grant of probate.

And how do you know probate has been granted? In a harmonious family situation, you’d expect to be notified of this but in the scenario you outline, it may be a case of your son keeping tabs on the Probate Register where all grants of probate and grants on administration (in case of intestacy) are recorded – along with copies of the related will where one exists.

He will need his father’s first and surname and the year in which he died.

When will probate be granted? That depends on how efficiently whoever is managing the estate sort the paperwork and how complex the estate is. It generally takes a year or close to it anyway.

Is it worth pursuing a section 117? That depends on your son’s position in life and also what his father’s estate comprises. There is certainly no guarantee of success and there will be legal fees to consider.

Of course, there is nothing to say that this money your ex has recently come into will still be part of his estate when he dies. It could well have been dissipated by then – either because it was spent or because it was gifted to other family members.

The Section 117 procedure only refers to provision in a will or lack thereof. It does not cover lifetime gifts.

]]><![CDATA[Opinion polls are core to how media covers politics, but is that a good thing?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/03/opinion-polls-are-core-to-how-media-covers-politics-but-is-that-a-good-thing/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/03/opinion-polls-are-core-to-how-media-covers-politics-but-is-that-a-good-thing/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000On Tuesday, Americans vote in midterm elections with consequences for everyone around the world. As usual, much of the campaign coverage has revolved around opinion polls, which give the Democrats a national lead of up to 11 points on the generic congressional ballot, while the party’s candidates are challenging for Senate seats in places where they usually wouldn’t have a hope.

Despite all that polling data, many remain sceptical about whether these predictions will be proved correct. Regardless, polls have been central to the coverage, as they are in most elections.

Polling has been a fixture of political journalism for almost 90 years. Its modern form dates from 1936, when George Gallup used a small but carefully chosen sample to predict Franklin Roosevelt’s landslide, humiliating the Literary Digest, whose vast survey of its own affluent readers had backed his opponent. Gallup’s results were syndicated to newspapers across the country, beginning a partnership between pollsters and the press that has lasted ever since.

But it was not until the 1970s, or in Ireland’s case the 1980s, that newspapers began to invest seriously in polls of their own. The Market Research Bureau of Ireland, founded by Jack Jones in 1962, spent years researching washing powder and air travel before turning to politics, and the Irish Times/MRBI series that began in the early 1980s became the benchmark here.

There has been no shortage of criticism of the relationship. Newspapers, it is suggested, over-dramatise results, splashing shouty headlines about tiny shifts that are within the margin of error. Polling is also blamed for “horse race” coverage that treats elections as sporting fixtures, ignoring the issues at stake. One Harvard study of the 2016 US presidential race found policy accounted for just a tenth of coverage, less than a quarter of the space devoted to who was ahead.

These criticisms are not without foundation, although research across 27 European countries suggests poll-driven coverage is most common in tight, multiparty contests, where knowing the state of play can help voters decide how to use their ballots.

Distrust of the polls themselves has also grown, with people pointing to glaring misses such as Brexit or Donald Trump’s first victory. That has been compounded by the rise of populist movements whose supporters are often underrepresented in surveys, prompting accusations of bias. Despite all this, a study of more than 200 elections in 32 countries found no evidence that polling errors were increasing.

Three elections in the past 10 days have highlighted some of these issues. In Brazil, the final surveys had incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead in the first round, which his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro edged, then gave Bolsonaro a narrow lead in the runoff, which Lula won by more than three points. Neither error was particularly large, but each picked the wrong winner.

In Israel, the final polls correctly predicted deadlock but underestimated both Likud and the Arab parties.

And in Serbia, where public polling is sparse and voters had reason to be wary of declaring opposition sympathies, surveys showing Aleksandar Vucic’s party narrowly ahead were proved completely wrong when the student-led opposition won an outright majority.

The Irish Times view on Serbia’s election: youthquake in Belgrade

Traditional polling is being reshaped by changes in the media industry. Falling revenues have made publishers less enthusiastic about the expensive business of high-quality polling. That has led to a move from face-to-face interviewing towards cheaper online panels, weighted to reflect the profile of the electorate.

In Ireland, Red C for the Business Post and Ireland Thinks for the Sunday Independent now alternate monthly online surveys, while The Irish Times’s face-to-face poll with Ipsos B&A appears several times a year. The methods can return somewhat different results. Red C, for example, regularly puts Fianna Fáil a few points lower than other pollsters do. But overall performance has been respectable, with final polls in 2024 largely within the margin of error. Every poll is a snapshot in time, and across volatile referendum campaigns, surveys and results have often diverged wildly.

The field has narrowed too, with titles such as the Sunday Times Irish edition no longer commissioning polls.

Elsewhere, there are signs of questionable standards. In September, an undercover investigation by Channel 4 News and the Verbatim group revealed that polls carried prominently by the Times and the Telegraph had been arranged by Reform UK figures and paid for through what they believed was an American donor’s company, without either paper being told.

In the US, a firm called Wedgewood Polls admitted last week that it had fabricated results reported by The New York Times, Newsweek and others. One Michigan Democratic candidate says a fake survey showing her in single digits drove away her donors and ended her Senate campaign.

The problem in both cases lay with news organisations failing to verify where the numbers came from and what financial incentives might have been involved. But what is even worse is that some US outlets are giving prominence to the almost completely unregulated prediction markets that have mushroomed in recent years. CNN and CNBC have partnerships with Kalshi, and Wall Street Journal owner Dow Jones with Polymarket, on undisclosed terms.

This seems a highly dubious proposition, since betting odds can be moved by anyone with deep enough pockets. The old model, in which media organisations paid for polls and stood over the results, may have had its flaws but this particular replacement looks considerably worse.

]]><![CDATA[Don’t make an additional voluntary contribution to your pension – until you read this]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000Retirement savers have just another two weeks or so until the November 18th deadline for tax relief on additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) for 2025 passes.

Often described as “turbo fuel” for your pension, the benefits of these payments are many. You can maximise available tax relief, improve your chances of retiring early, and you’ll hopefully have a bigger fund to draw down in retirement thanks to them.

But before you lock your money away through AVCs, it’s also worth taking a moment to consider if they are the best option for your money at a particular point in time.

Your money is locked away

Once you put additional money into your pension, it is locked away until you can retire. But what if you need it for your health? Your children? To pay down expensive debts? Repairs on your house, or just for those holidays you want to take now, rather than wait until retirement?

“It’s really a case of having a financial plan – and prioritising what’s most important,” says Mark Ryan, director of My Wealth Management.

Putting money into the stock market, an investment fund, or a high-yielding deposit account can still give you the potential for real gains, while maintaining flexibility. Of course, you are giving up on the tax relief – but this might be okay.

“Tax relief, while it’s great, shouldn’t be the only consideration. It’s of little benefit if it leaves you short of money for other needs,” says Sinead McEvoy, head of retirement solutions at Standard Life.

For McEvoy, a solid approach can be doing “a bit of both”. Put some money into a rainy-day fund, for example, and some into an AVC.

She is often asked whether or not you should prioritise your pension, or paying your mortgage.

Managing your money and your time in retirement

For some, the psychological impact of paying off a mortgage is huge, and this can take priority when it comes to spare cash. But focusing on it solely may not be the right approach either.

“I don’t think I’d pay off all your mortgage and ignore your pension,” she says. “Think of all the compounding you’re missing out on by paying off your mortgage.”

“It would be a preference for some people,” Ryan agrees, referring to paying down the mortgage first. Another option, he suggests, is to boost your AVCs now, and hope for investment growth, and use the bigger lump sum when you retire to pay down the mortgage at that point.

You won’t benefit from the same tax relief as AVCs by paying down your mortgage, so it can be worthwhile to “crunch the numbers” before making a decision.

Indeed, there can be an opportunity cost of this approach; you are giving up on tax relief, which can supercharge your pension fund.

Consider €200 invested every month for 10 years. If it returns an average of 6 per cent a year, it will deliver almost €32,500. But if tax relief had been available, at the higher rate, you would have had €280 going into the investment each month – so the return would have been significantly higher, at €45,500. You just wouldn’t have been able to withdraw it.

You may end up paying a higher tax rate in retirement

“I get asked this question often,” says Ryan. “Why would I put in money to get tax relief at 40 per cent when I pay it at the same rate in retirement?”

Remember, the tax relief you enjoy on AVCs is only deferred; when you draw down your pension, you may pay income tax on it. So then, you need to bear in mind the value of this tax relief – while it will grow tax-free, which is very beneficial, it can be particularly valuable if you get relief on it today as a higher rate taxpayer, and draw it down at the standard rate of tax in retirement.

While a higher tax rate in retirement is indicative of a healthy fund, it may be a consideration for those close to the higher tax bracket.

“Those on the borderline (of the higher rate), and considering AVCs, then it’s a conversation worth having,” says Ryan. “I have had scenarios where people have decided not to do AVCs because of that.”

Others, however, will opt for the ‘bird in the hand’ approach, and take what’s on offer now – tax relief – rather than predict how the future might play out.

This decision may be only for a certain cohort, however. First of all, to maximise your tax-free lump sum on retirement of €200,000, you will need a fund of €800,000 – 25 per cent is tax-free; amounts between €200,000 and €500,000 are taxed at 20 per cent. “And that’s a significant pension fund for most,” says McEvoy. “Typically, people are underfunding their pensions.”

Lessons for a happy retirement from a year interviewing Ireland’s top leaders

So, paying in AVCs can help bump up your tax-free lump sum.

And, paying tax at the higher rate on your pension “just isn’t the case for most people” says McEvoy, pointing to the more generous tax bands available for the over-65s.

As our table shows, a married couple with an annual pension income of €36,126 won’t pay any tax in retirement, while single people aged 65 and over won’t pay tax on earnings of less than €18,000.

However, as income rises, retirees will see a growing proportion of their income taxed at the higher rate. A single person earning €45,563 from a combination of state pension and private pension income, for example, will pay a certain portion of their income at the higher rate of 40 per cent (€1,563 for 2026), thus pushing their effective rate up to 12.3 per cent. And it increases from there; someone earning €75,563 a year in retirement will pay the top rate of tax on €31, 563 of their income – for an effective tax rate of 24.5 per cent.

AVCs have to be drawn down at the same time as an occupational pension

Having different pension vehicles in play may give you greater flexibility as to when you have to draw down your pension. PRSAs (Personal Retirement Savings Accounts), for example, can be drawn down between 60 – or 50 if it isn’t tied to an employment – and 75. It might also help keep your pension income in retirement taxed at the lower rate.

Remember, however AVCs are funded – either through the main scheme or an AVC PRSA – they are tied to this main scheme.

“When you have an AVC, it must be retired at the same time as the main scheme,” says McEvoy. So, there is no flexibility available when putting your AVC money into a separate pension vehicle.

However, there might be the opportunity to segment your pension into different PRSAs at retirement, so that you can draw them down at different ages.

There is some flexibility, however, if you’re not happy with the fund choices offered in your occupational/public sector scheme.

AVC PRSAs can be used to offer greater investment choice. But the charges might be higher than in your occupational scheme, so this should be considered.

What are AVCs?

In short, AVCs are additional payments you make to your occupational or public sector pension to boost your fund, and hopefully your income in retirement.

If you have already maximised your matching contributions (ie, your employer contributes 6 per cent of salary if you contribute 6 per cent), and you have extra cash, you can consider putting this into your pension via an AVC.

As with all pension savings, the big advantage here is the tax relief you get – if you’re a higher rate taxpayer, for example, a €1,000 contribution to your pension will only cost you €600.

How much you can contribute and avail of tax relief will depend on Revenue limits. Tax relief is offered as a percentage of your net earnings, and increases in line with your age. So, if you’re aged between 30 and 39, for example, you can put 20 per cent of your earnings into your pension and get tax relief on it (so up to €10,000 a year if you earn €50,000, for example). This percentage increases to 30 per cent for those aged 50-54; 35 per cent for 55-59; and 40 per cent for 60 and over.

When it comes to making an AVC, you can do so on a regular or one-off basis, so they offer good flexibility. A maximum annual limit of €115,000 applies.

If you haven’t made AVCs for 2025, and you do so before the online tax return deadline of November 18th, you will be due a tax saving.

]]>Collins Photos<![CDATA[New EU charge to push up prices for many online shoppers]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/new-eu-charge-set-to-see-prices-spike-for-many-online-shoppers/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/new-eu-charge-set-to-see-prices-spike-for-many-online-shoppers/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:57:29 +0000Parcels arriving in Ireland from outside of the European Union will be hit with charges of at least €5 per item as a result of two distinct fees that are now applied.

The new €2 “Union Handling Fee” that came into effect on Sunday is on top of a €3 customs charge per item that was introduced earlier this year.

The charges and fees are mandated at EU level, with delivery companies given the legal responsibility to collect them if the levies have not been paid during online checkout.

The new charge is intended to cover the increased costs incurred by customs authorities due to the huge growth of ecommerce in recent years. It will apply to all goods, regardless of their value, once a seller ships them to Ireland from outside the EU.

The growth in online marketplaces – based in China primarily – has caused dramatic upheaval in retail. According to official estimates, about six billion packages with a value of less than €150 came into EU states from outside the bloc last year.

New charges mean online shopping is now a lot more expensive

The EU handling fee of €2 per item adds a further €6 to the bill, bringing the total end cost to €25.

Consumers will be expected to pay the charges in one of two ways.

Some larger ecommerce operations will be set up to collect the customs duty and EU handling fee at the point of sale.

In such circumstances, both charges will be shown to the consumer and the total price paid at the checkout will be the final price, with no extra charges on delivery.

Other websites may not collect these charges at checkout and the delivery company will be required to collect the money from the consumer.

When charges have to be collected in this way it is likely a further administrative fee of about €7 will be added to the total by the delivery company.

A forthcoming Journal of Finance paper, Disposed to Be Overconfident, suggests profit-taking can distort our memories and judgment.

When judging their stock-picking abilities, ordinary investors rarely bother with overall portfolio returns or comparisons with the market. Instead, the study says, they use a simpler scorecard: how many stocks they sold at a profit versus how many sold at a loss.

By selling winners quickly, holding on to losers, and remembering the former more fondly, investors convince themselves they are better stock-pickers than their overall returns suggest.

The researchers found evidence of how skewed this scorecard can be. Ordinary Dutch investors recalled selling an average of 4.22 stocks at a profit over a year, almost twice the 2.17 recorded in their trading histories.

In a subsequent experiment, traders who were forced to sell winning stocks became more confident of their abilities than those forced to sell losers. And yet, the two groups picked virtually the same number of winning stocks and made almost identical overall profits. Simply realising a profit made people feel more skilful than they really were.

Fake news: why investors keep believing stories they know are false

The researchers link this to the disposition effect, the tendency to sell winners too early while hanging on to losers. The resulting scorecard is flattering, with profits banked and remembered, while losses remain unrealised and out of sight.

However, it can drive a vicious cycle: profit-taking builds overconfidence, which encourages over-trading, which degrades wealth through bad timing and transaction fees.

Our pleasure in hearing the cash register ring is natural. However, the sound of money being banked doesn’t mean we know what we’re doing.

Much of the global debate about AI has focused on the foundations of the technology: energy, chips, data centres and large AI models. Those layers do matter and Ireland already has significant assets in technology infrastructure.

For Ireland, however, the greatest opportunity may lie higher up the value chain in the application layer, the applications that turn AI capability into useful products and services for particular industries.

Where Ireland Can Compete

Ireland already has considerable expertise in sectors where AI could change how complex businesses operate, including technology, financial services, life sciences and healthcare. Businesses here do not need to build the next frontier model to create valuable AI intellectual property. They can combine their knowledge of those industries with increasingly capable AI tools to develop products that their clients will actually use and which can solve real commercial problems.

The investment environment is also encouraging.

Pitchbook data records €947.3 million across 182 Irish AI deals since January 2025, including €256 million across 75 deals so far in 2026. It places Ireland second in Europe for AI venture-capital deal count per capita.

More than $250m invested in Irish artificial intelligence firms over first half of 2026

The challenge is to ensure that this activity translates into businesses, intellectual property, specialist employment and economic value that remain in Ireland. None of this will be straightforward.

Energy and infrastructure pressures cannot be ignored, competition for skilled people is intense and other European countries are pursuing the same investment.

Regulatory complexity can also affect where new products are tested and commercialised. That makes it all the more important that Ireland focuses on areas where its existing strengths give it an advantage, rather than trying to replicate the scale of AI infrastructure being developed elsewhere.

Getting Regulation Right

Regulation is part of that picture. Ireland should not have to choose between having effective regulation or having a competitive AI sector. The backing of the Dublin Declaration on trustworthy, safe and sovereign artificial intelligence by EU member states reflects an important principle: trusted AI and competitiveness should reinforce rather than undermine one another.

The Startup Ireland AI Accelerator Programme and the additional €45 million announced for technology centres by 2030 are welcome signals too. But the test will be whether those commitments on policy, investment and regulation work in practice.

Ireland can capture the AI dividend while mitigating the risks

Businesses developing new AI products need to understand how the rules apply and have the opportunity to engage with regulators at an early stage. Regulators have an important role to play in providing that clarity and helping businesses navigate the regulatory framework as new products are developed. Making that work in practice will require sufficient resources and technical expertise within Ireland’s regulators, as well as effective co-ordination between the AI Office of Ireland, the Data Protection Commission and other relevant authorities.

The proposed AI Regulatory Sandbox could also play an important role if it gives businesses practical access to regulators as they move from testing their new products to bringing them to market.

This is not an argument for lighter regulation. Trust matters, particularly in sectors such as financial services and life sciences, and the importance of maintaining trust while supporting innovation was a recurring theme at the International AI Summit.

Ireland’s opportunity is to show that effective regulation and innovation can work together. Businesses need to understand the rules and be able to engage constructively with regulators as new products are developed. Regulation should protect people properly, while being sufficiently clear and proportionate to support investment and the development of new technologies in Ireland.

Ireland’s position in the AI economy is not accidental. It reflects many years of investment, international business experience and accumulated technology expertise. But we should not assume that those advantages will automatically carry over into AI.

Having secured a place in the global AI ecosystem, the question now is whether Ireland remains principally a location where AI is hosted, regulated and consumed, or whether it becomes one where the next generation of AI businesses and applications is built.

The countries that succeed in capturing those added-value investments will shape the next decade of economic growth. Ireland has every opportunity to be among them.

Marie McGinley is a partner and head of the technology and innovation group at Matheson LLP

]]>dem10<![CDATA[In its rush to curb China, the EU could learn lessons from Ireland’s protectionist past]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/02/in-its-rush-to-curb-china-the-eu-could-learn-lessons-from-irelands-protectionist-past/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/02/in-its-rush-to-curb-china-the-eu-could-learn-lessons-from-irelands-protectionist-past/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000After the nightmare of the second World War, the recovering economies of Europe built a free trade world. The European Economic Community (EEC), founded in 1958, embodied the commitment to more openness. Ireland, however, slept, with a highly protected and expensive, inefficient domestic manufacturing sector.

In the 1930s, along with most other countries, we introduced protectionist measures to develop domestic industry. These remained in place into the 1960s when Seán Lemass gradually dismantled the trade barriers in anticipation of EEC entry, which we joined in 1973.

The maintenance of protection after the war had not resulted in successful Irish businesses. The process of moving to free trade proved painful. Much of the existing industry could not compete and shut down in the late 1960s and 1970s. It took time for new firms, many foreign-owned, to establish themselves and to reap the benefits of EU market access. This move to free trade eventually proved hugely beneficial for Ireland; it was just a pity it had not happened 20 years earlier.

This experience has lessons for the EU today. The rise of China as a significant world manufacturing centre benefiting from government subsidies, along with hostile and erratic US policy to its trading partners, has sharply altered the world trade order.

These factors have evoked a misguided EU response, of trying to protect domestic manufacturing through raising barriers to trade and “buy EU” regulations. In the long term, freer trade is the best answer, and can raise living standards for all partners. Even in time, the US may come to realise it.

The EU’s policy response of protecting EU firms needs an exit strategy: a reformed business sector must be able to compete again on the world stage. There is a serious danger that the EU could lock itself into an increasingly inefficient and costly world of its own.

The changed external environment came at a time when EU factories were already under pressure. In 2008-2024 EU manufacturing employment fell by 1.5 million. However, 4.5 million people without a degree lost their jobs, while graduate employment went up by 3 million.

The significant loss of jobs among less qualified workers is having significant political consequences and fuelling the successes of Germany’s AfD and Marine Le Pen’s prospect of becoming French president.

France has been particularly badly hit. Some 800,000 lower-skilled manufacturing jobs have gone, and the rise of 200,000 graduate jobs has not compensated. In Germany the increase of 800,000 graduate jobs has almost counterbalanced the loss of 900,000 jobs among those without a degree.

Faced with a world hostile to free trade, a different approach is needed to produce a vibrant and successful EU manufacturing sector. Policy interventions should aim to help EU manufacturing to transition to a world where it can stand on its own feet.

Temporary protection should only be accorded to sectors that have a realistic chance of being able to sell in a global market within a reasonable time scale. Protecting an EU car industry that in future can only sell on a protected EU market would be a strategic mistake.

China leads in battery production and solar panels, not just because of government support, or its ready access to rare earths. It’s because the Chinese have engaged in successful research in materials science, resulting in big changes in battery and solar panel efficiency. If China were selling shoddy products at low prices, that wouldn’t be a problem for potential competitors.

The EU should not give up its ambition to have a strong manufacturing sector offering good jobs. However, it will need to invest in research and innovation to transform EU manufacturing into a world-class supplier.

The drastic cuts by the US government to funding for pharmaceutical research have opened the opportunity for the EU to move into that gap. That could prove a real winner. Such research is key to global pharmaceutical innovation. At the same time, China is coming up on the outside and is investing in this area of research. To make the breakthrough for Europe and be successful, research and innovation in pharmaceuticals must take place on an EU scale. Fragmented research efforts country by country won’t bring the critical mass needed.

Given the changing profile of today’s and tomorrow’s manufacturing businesses, the EU also needs to invest in upskilling its workforce. New businesses and new sectors will need different skills from the past. The capacity to adapt and possession of readily transferable skills can give European workers a new edge.

Almost eight out of 10 Irish workers want annual leave increased, according to a study by FRS Recruitment, which questioned 300 people about their use of holidays.

But 43 per cent of workers fail to use their full annual leave entitlements, with some missing out on up to one week’s holiday.

Many of them choose to carry leave entitlements over to the following year, but some opt for payment in lieu of the time off that they do not take.

However, 12 per cent end up losing their unused annual leave days, the study found.

FRS Recruitment general manager Lynne McCormack branded the trend worrying, saying that number had increased since last year’s survey.

“Time off from work is necessary for people to manage their wellbeing and these findings raise concerns that annual leave is not being used effectively,” she said.

Most workers want more flexible annual leave terms from their employers, the survey shows. In addition, 84 per cent said that time taken off at Christmas should be separated from their annual leave entitlements.

Almost 60 per cent want unlimited annual leave, FRS Recruitment found, while 18 per cent take more than two weeks off.

‘Fertility treatment is like a second job’: How can employers support staff undergoing IVF?

Listening to employees’ expectations and keeping policies up to date will become increasingly important for businesses trying to keep staff, McCormack said.

Most Irish people use their annual leave to travel abroad, with many heading to Spain, Portugal or Italy for their holidays. Other destinations, including the United States, Southeast Asia and Australia, also feature.

Outside of work, people take leave for family, health and personal reasons, the FRS Recruitment Annual Leave Report, published on Monday, found.

The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski.

However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”.

Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend.

PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026

The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control.

Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska.

For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present.

However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed.

 

The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges.

None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached.

They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges.

That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached.

Zgromadzenie Ogólne TK: JEST KWORUM! 👏
Według przedstawionej interpretacji liczy się je od 12 uprawnionych osób. 2/3 × 12 = 8.
Prawo i matematyka.👏 pic.twitter.com/77v2ep9HbT

— Pani Prezes 👠 (@PaniNaSzpilkach) November 3, 2026

Once that issue was agreed, the eight judges present proceeded to decide upon a number of key issues. First, they adopted a draft budget for the TK for 2027, something that Święczkowski had been unable to achieve, which was used as an argument for his ousting.

Second, they drew lots to decide which of the TK’s judges would sit on disciplinary panels for Święczkowski and Sochański in relation to their suspension from the court.

However, some legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether a legal quorum was established at today’s meeting. Ryszard Piotrowski, a prominent constitutional scholar, called the meeting “illegal”, reports news website Onet. Przemysław Rosati, the president of the Supreme Bar Council, also expressed his doubts.

Obniżenie progu kworum na skutek zawieszenia prezesa i wiceprezesa otwiera puszkę Pandory. To jest mechanizm, który pozwala dowolnie obniżać kworum na Zgromadzeniu Ogólnym TK – wystarczy, że prezes zawiesi 10 sędziów i będzie mógł na Zgromadzeniu podejmować decyzję w trzy osoby.…

— Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) November 3, 2026

Święczkowski himself rejected the legitimacy of what he called a “social gathering”, saying that Korwin-Piotrowska is a “usurper” who has no right to call a general assembly at all, reported Polsat News.

Shortly before the meeting at the TK, Nawrocki also met with the prime minister, Donald Tusk, for the first time since the crisis at the court broke out last Friday. They had convened at the presidential palace for a meeting of the National Security Council that Nawrocki had called before the TK crisis.

During public remarks broadcast before the confidential meeting got underway, Nawrocki accused the government of “illegally taking over the Constitutional Tribunal”. He added that Tusk “bears full responsibility for…all these illegal actions”.

Grubo! Karol Nawrocki do Tuska:

„Pełną odpowiedzialność za wszystkie nielegalne działa w Trybunale Konstytucyjnym ponosi jeden człowiek, który jest obecny – premier Donald Tusk” pic.twitter.com/WMPnWTZIKt

— chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 3, 2026

Tusk and his government have argued that the source of the crisis is, in fact, Nawrocki’s refusal to swear in judges appointed by parliament, as he is required to do, and then Święczkowski’s resultant refusal to accept those judges onto the court.

They also note that the TK has not been legitimate for a decade, since PiS unlawfully appointed judges and brought the court under its political influence.

Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Tuesday before the general assembly, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that the actions being undertaken by Korwin-Piotrowska are the only way “to rebuild the independence of the tribunal”.

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026

According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget.

He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits.

Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. He says they may be tempted to “interfere with electricity bills” and that “it is therefore quite likely that certain charges (e.g. the distribution charge) will be reduced in 2027”.

Komisja Europejska wrzuciła dane o cenach prądu za I półrocze 2026 roku i – boy, oh, boy – niesamowita jest to lektura.

Na początek mocne uderzenie: w ujęciu standardu siły nabywczej polskie gospodarstwa domowe mają drugie najwyższe ceny prądu w całej Unii Europejskiej.… pic.twitter.com/yKvt5251i7

— Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) November 1, 2026

Energy prices and the wider energy transition have already become increasingly politicised this year, with the right-wing opposition criticising EU climate policies.

The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, recently called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS, claiming that it treats “Poles as a cash machine for the absurd leftist climate policy of the EU”.

Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has twice attempted to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policy, but in both cases his proposals were rejected by the more pro-EU government’s majority in parliament.

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed.

Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information.

On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good.

In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance.

In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.

The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.

The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.

In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:59:45 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Why Virgin Media O2 is cutting jobs and retreating from fibre https://www.cityam.com/why-virgin-media-o2-is-cutting-jobs-and-retreating-from-fibre/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:59:35 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474234

Virgin Media O2’s decision to cut thousands of jobs and halt further fibre upgrades marks quite the retreat for a company once positioned as BT’s biggest challenger, writes Saskia Koopman. Five years after Virgin Media and O2 merged to create a £31bn telecoms giant, VMO2 is battling falling revenues, ongoing customer losses and over £22bn [...]]]>

Virgin Media O2’s decision to cut thousands of jobs and halt further fibre upgrades marks quite the retreat for a company once positioned as BT’s biggest challenger, writes Saskia Koopman.

Five years after Virgin Media and O2 merged to create a £31bn telecoms giant, VMO2 is battling falling revenues, ongoing customer losses and over £22bn of debt. Its response? An £800m annual cost-cutting programme, including £300m in workforce savings and a halt to further full-fibre upgrades beyond existing commitments.

But the restructuring also exposes wider issues in Britain’s broadband industry, where years of network investment have left operators competing for customers in an increasingly saturated market.

A merger under pressure

When Liberty Global and Telefónica combined their UK businesses in 2021, the aim was to create a stronger competitor to BT by combining Virgin Media’s broadband infrastructure and O2’s mobile network.

The deal, however, also saddled the firm with heavy debt. Additional borrowing to establish the 50/50 ownership structure meant VMO2 was born with around £18bn of it. Higher interest rates have also since added to the pressure, and five years and more than £10bn of investment later, the company is cutting, rather than expanding, its network.

The group’s third-quarter revenue fell 5.7 per cent to £2.4bn, while underlying earnings declined 2.6 per cent. It also shed over 22,000 broadband connections.

Paolo Pescatore, analyst at PP Foresight, described the restructuring as a potential “last roll of the dice to rebuild confidence”.

“Simplification is overdue, but the scale of the changes raises uncomfortable questions about what the merger has delivered”, he said.

“Employees now face the consequences of a business still searching for a convincing route to sustainable growth”.

Most redundancies are expected to affect non-customer-facing roles, while VMO2 is increasing its use of AI in customer service and sales.

The Communication Workers Union warned that losing experienced staff could undermine service quality. “It is important that immediate cost savings do not have a negative long-term impact by losing workers with the key skills and legacy knowledge that is so crucial to ensuring good customer service”, said assistant secretary Stephen Albon.

The group’s fibre ambitions

VMO2’s decision to halt further full-fibre upgrades also reflects mounting pressure across the industry, where years of investment have created overlapping networks. BT’s Openreach is competing against Virgin Media, as well as smaller providers including Cityfibre, Community Fibre and Gigaclear.

While competition has expanded consumer choice, operators are also facing borrowing costs and pressure to attract customers to justify spend.

VMO2 has now concluded that the market just cannot support three overlapping fibre networks. Instead of continuing its full-fibre upgrade programme, the company is planning to use cheaper technology to deliver speeds of up to 2Gbps across most of its remaining cable networks by 2027.

It is also reportedly nearing a deal to use BT’s Openreach infrastructure to reach customers outside its existing footprint. This would mark a change of direction for a company whose shareholders have backed nexfibre as a major challenger to Openreach.

The shift comes as the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) considers whether to block nexfibre’s proposed £2bn acquisition of Netomnia.

VMO2’s shareholders have accused regulators of inconsistency after BT was allowed to rescue struggling rival Talktalk, while their own deal faces competition concerns.

Meanwhile, CityFibre is negotiating a refinancing after accumulating £3.9bn in net debt, underlining the financial pressures facing alternative broadband providers.

Will the cuts be enough?

VMO2 is not alone in reducing its headcount, with BT having announced plans in 2023 to cut as many as 55,000 jobs by 2030, and VodafoneThree also pursuing redundancies.

But VMO2’s debt burden makes its restructuring plans more urgent than perhaps its rivals’.

Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Erhan Gurses estimates the redundancies could generate around £200m in annual gross savings by 2028.

“Yet it wouldn’t effectively resolve the balance-sheet strain”, he added, warning that the net leverage would still be around 5.5 times earnings in 2028, above the firm’s target range of four to five times.

“Preserving cash is understandable”, Pescatore added. “However, pulling back on fibre risks weakening differentiation over time”.

“A smaller cost base means little if customers and revenue keep shrinking”.

VMO2’s difficult challenge will be cutting spending without also accelerating the customer losses that have so far contributed to its financial difficulties.

The company is expected to set out its fuller strategy alongside its annual results in early 2027.

The fact there’s another qualifier at Newbury on Thursday, with several of these runners doubly declared, means you can whittle the field down significantly.

SATURDAY’S November Handicap from Doncaster is the traditional curtain closer to the domestic Flat season.

This meeting is often run in attritional conditions but with the dry weather we’ve had all summer, the ground may be unseasonably quick on Town Moor this weekend.

My main bet on the card comes in the Listed Wentworth Stakes (2.10pm), where I think COUL ANGEL can land a hat-trick of wins on ground conditions that should be ideal for him.

Mick Appleby’s gelding has proven himself to be highly progressive in his last two starts, winning a competitive handicap at the Curragh by nearly three lengths and then landing another nice handicap pot at York last time.

The form of that York contest has worked out well, with the second and third-placed horses both coming out and winning since.

He has shot up a stone in the ratings after those two wins and, now rated 108, looks well worth his place in Listed company.

His likely main danger, Montassib, is now an eight-year-old and it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Coul Angel improve past him.

Joanna Mason, who rode him to win at York last time, retains the ride and at 9/2 he’s a very solid bet.

Softer conditions than she encountered throughout the summer might just suit Ed Walker’s FELICITAS in the Listed Gillies Fillies’ Stakes (2.45pm).

She has never run on officially soft ground, but her first two starts in the spring came on ground with a bit of cut and included an excellent effort when a close up second in the Musidora at York.

Following that, her sights were raised when she wasn’t disgraced behind Diamond Necklace in the Group One Prix de Diane.

She returned having been off the track since August, when running a good race to finish fourth in Group Three company at Newmarket last month.

That start should have brought her forward and a good run can be expected at 6/1.

The day’s big betting race is the £75,000 feature November Handicap (3.25pm).

Current favourite NOBODY KNOWS is very lightly raced for trainer Richard Hughes and there’s a fair chance he could be well-handicapped.

He won his first two starts, which included a novice on soft ground at Ayr at the back end of last season and then at Wolverhampton on his reappearance this campaign.

He was beaten less than a length on handicap debut over a mile at Sandown in the spring, before he ran most recently at York last month, which followed a long break.

It looks as though connections have had their eyes on this prize for a while and that run should have left him spot on for it.

He steps up to a mile-and-a-half for the first time, which should bring about improvement, and the booking of Ryan Moore is a major signal of intent.

I can see him going off a good deal shorter than his current price of 4/1 on the day, making him good ante-post value, and it would be no surprise if he proved too good for his rivals.

Another I’m keen to throw into the mix at bigger odds is LORD MELBOURNE.

Ralph Beckett’s six-year-old won this race two years ago and has been slowly working down the handicap this season.

He arrives here after finishing a close third at York recently and now with Harry Vigors claiming five pounds in the saddle, he looks on a dangerous mark.

Conditions are no worry, and 12/1 is a fair each-way price.

Coul Angel                                       2.10pm               Doncaster

Felcitas e/w                                     2.45pm               Doncaster

Nobody Knows                               3.25pm               Doncaster

Lord Melbourne e/w                     3.25pm               Doncaster

]]> 2474163Bill Esdaile Bill Esdaile City watchdog ‘stands ready’ to act on bank windfall tax Budget leak https://www.cityam.com/city-watchdog-stands-ready-to-act-on-bank-windfall-tax-budget-leak/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:31:18 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474102

The boss of the Financial Conduct Authority has said he is prepared to investigate a potential leak of market-sensitive information that sparked a rally in bank shares hours before John Healey’s maiden Budget. In a letter to the Treasury Committee, Nikhil Rathi vowed to engage with Treasury and Cabinet Office officials over how the details [...]]]>

The boss of the Financial Conduct Authority has said he is prepared to investigate a potential leak of market-sensitive information that sparked a rally in bank shares hours before John Healey’s maiden Budget.

In a letter to the Treasury Committee, Nikhil Rathi vowed to engage with Treasury and Cabinet Office officials over how the details of the Chancellor’s windfall tax on banks ended up in the press, and whether “any unlawful disclosure of inside information may have occurred”.

The watchdog chief wrote that parliamentary scrutiny like select committees and leak inquiries were usually a preferred process for “passing judgment on political discourse and government communications”.

But he added the City’s top regulator may “choose to intervene where that discourse, or poor information handling, impacts markets improperly”.

“We stand ready to consider the specifics of any evidence provided to us by Cabinet Office and HMT to decide what, if any, action it is appropriate for us to take,” he said.

Rathi was responding to a letter that Meg Hillier wrote last week, in which the Treasury Committee chair asked whether an apparent leak of the windfall tax’s severity constituted an “improper release of inside information”.

Shares in high-street lenders surged in the hours leading up to the Budget, after Bloomberg News revealed the heavily trailed banks surcharge would only be temporary and not be as high as some had speculated. Lloyds and Natwest shares climbed as much as four per cent before the levy was formally announced, while Barclays jumped 3.7 per cent.

“This appears to have been more than idle speculation,” Hillier wrote in her initial letter, “and it has implications for relevant securities.”

Reeves Budget sparks Treasury probe

Last year, preparations for Rachel Reeves’ final Budget were plunged into disarray by a wave of leaks and briefings. The then-Chancellor made a speech preparing voters for a manifesto-busting income tax rise – before pulling back from the idea amid pressure from Number 10. Policies including a freezing of income tax thresholds, a levy on electric vehicles and a tourist tax all became public knowledge in the pre-Budget period, and the decision to abort the income tax plans sparked a sharp jump in gilt yields.

The rampant speculation prompted the Treasury to launch an inquiry into the leaks. Minister James Murray said the probe, which reported in February this year, would investigate the “security processes to inform future fiscal events”.

In a parallel letter to Treasury permanent secretary James Bowler, Hillier said it would be “deeply concerning” if the leaks were unauthorised given government efforts to tighten Budget security.

She also asked Bowler to confirm that neither banks – nor their trade bodies – were told of the changes “in outline or with specifics” before the Budget, and to reveal how many people had prior access to the policy’s final structure. The Treasury has not responded to the committee’s letter.

]]> 2474102Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Barclays and HSBC bankers donate over $500k in US midterms https://www.cityam.com/barclays-and-hsbc-bankers-donate-over-500k-in-us-midterms/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:29:47 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474140

Barclays and HSBC bankers donated over half a million dollars to US political candidates ahead of the midterm elections. Bankers who are employed at the two UK-headquartered giants flooded cash into US political figures as  millions of Americans headed to the polls. Donors listing Barclays or one of its subsidiaries as an employer contributed just [...]]]>

Barclays and HSBC bankers donated over half a million dollars to US political candidates ahead of the midterm elections.

Bankers who are employed at the two UK-headquartered giants flooded cash into US political figures as  millions of Americans headed to the polls.

Donors listing Barclays or one of its subsidiaries as an employer contributed just over $344k (£256k) to candidates since the beginning of 2025, according to Federal Election Commission figures. 

Chief among those was a whopping $70k from the investment bank’s banking chairman Alexander Lynch, whose sum was sent to the House Victory Project, a fund split across Democrat candidates.

HSBC staff donated over $163k, according to FEC data. This was led by Mark Schuermann, head of public affairs in the US, who donated around $18k to the bank’s Political Action Committee (PAC).

The group has different PACs which are financed by voluntary employee donations. This pooled money is kept separately and is isolated from company profits to comply with campaign laws. 

A HSBC spokesperson said: “HSBC Political Action Committees are committees formed by eligible employees and they are not controlled by HSBC nor use HSBC funds.”

They added the committees operate in a “bipartisan manner contributing to candidates of all political parties” and seek to ensure “an even split between parties”.

The bank focuses its US operations on international commercial banking, wealth management, and wholesale markets. It has major coastal hubs like New York, San Francisco and Miami.

US gears up for ‘referendum on Trump’

Of the big four UK banks, Barclays and HSBC have the greatest presence in the US. Individuals listing Natwest and Lloyds Banking Group as their employers donated around $5k collectively.

Barclays operates a major investment banking and corporate presence based out of New York. It also has a targeted consumer business focused primarily on co-branded credit cards with American airlines and retailers. 

A Barclays spokesperson said the bank is a “politically neutral organisation and does not engage in party political campaigning or make party political donations”.

They added that colleagues involved in political activity in a personal capacity have “a responsibility to make sure that this is kept entirely separate from their duties as an employee” and that Barclays’ funds are not used for political purposes.

The US midterms will contest all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 out of the 100 in the US senate. 

It is broadly expected to be fought on issues around the economy with many pollsters viewing the elections as a referendum on Donald Trump.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent in September 2026, above market expectations and up from 3.4 per cent in each of the previous two months.

]]> 2474140Samuel Norman Samuel Norman Asda’s turnaround king names heir to the throne https://www.cityam.com/asdas-turnaround-king-names-heir-to-the-throne/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:19:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474176

Allan Leighton was adamant. Just two months ago, Asda’s then-executive chairman insisted that his position as the sole leader of the discount grocer’s turnaround plans would not change any time soon.  It had been rumoured that Asda was on the lookout for a chief executive to bolster its efforts to return to its heyday, but [...]]]>

Allan Leighton was adamant. Just two months ago, Asda’s then-executive chairman insisted that his position as the sole leader of the discount grocer’s turnaround plans would not change any time soon. 

It had been rumoured that Asda was on the lookout for a chief executive to bolster its efforts to return to its heyday, but Leighton told City AM that any changes of leadership were “not imminent”. 

And when any change of leadership finally arrived, he said, it would come from within Asda’s existing top team. “The preference would be to appoint a CEO from inside the company, and we have a very highly talented group of executives, and my hope is that somebody would emerge from the group,” he had said. 

Just weeks later Leighton has already handed over the top job – to an outsider. David Potts, a former boss of rival Morrisons, took the reins as chief executive role with immediate effect, prompting Leighton to step back into a non-executive chairman position. 

This apparent U-turn was “unexpected but not entirely surprising,” independent retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth said. Asda has been searching on-and-off for a chief executive since the departure of Roger Burnley in 2021. 

Petrol station tycoon Mohsin Issa, who bought the grocer from US retail giant Walmart for £6.8bn in 2021, was Asda’s boss until September 2024 but the group has been without a chief executive since Leighton’s appointment as executive chairman. 

While Leighton said he was looking inwards to find his successor after exhausting his external search, the Asda chairman told the Times that he had been pursuing Potts all along. 

“I have been patient. I have got the right person,” he said. “His experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him.”

Asda and Morrisons fight for recovery

Potts’s appointment comes only two years after Leighton returned to Asda to lead its comeback. He had been the grocer’s marketing director and later its chief executive during its 1990s heyday, when he and Marks & Spencer chairman Archie Norman oversaw its blockbuster sale to Walmart.

Asda’s current owners, private equity firm TDR Capital, looked to Leighton to inject some much-needed energy into the grocer in November 2024, when it was facing an existential threat from the insurgent discount supermarket chains Aldi and Lidl.

Known for his penchant for showmanship, Leighton once rode into an annual managers’ conference by revving into the auditorium on a Harley Davidson motorcycle.

Potts, on the other hand, is an “operational leader,” Shuttleworth said, who will likely be focussed on the minutiae of shoppers’ in-store experience. The move will see him reunited with finance chief Michael Gleeson, who he worked with during his stints at both Tesco and Morrisons. 

Though Potts will take charge of the day-to-day running of Asda, the supermarket chain said Leighton will remain involved in the group’s long-term planning, as it attempts to mount a charge up the grocery sector’s market share league table. 

Asda is currently the UK’s third-largest grocer, holding 11.5 per cent of the market, though this share has dropped from the 11.8 per cent it held this time last year, as Aldi and Lidl threaten to add to their 10.5 and 8.6 per cent shares.

Potts takes up ‘difficult’ task

Josh Holmes, head of research at Retail Economics, said: “The appointment may have surprised people, but there’s a clear commercial logic to it. Potts’s early turnaround at Morrisons centred on competitive prices, better availability and stronger service. Those are precisely the areas Asda needs to get right.”

There are similarities between Asda and Morrisons, its closest rival. Both are private-equity owned, both have faced intense competition from the German discounters in recent years and both are being weighed down by billions of pounds of debt. 

Though Asda slumped to a £989m pre-tax loss last year it did manage to slim down its debt pile by £500m, to £3.1bn. Morrisons, however, saw its net debt rise last year from £7.1bn to £7.5bn.

Morrisons has made more progress towards its turnaround than Asda, having posted 15 consecutive quarters of sales growth under the stewardship of Rami Batiéh, Potts’s successor. 

“Potts inherits a difficult job. Asda has lost ground while competitors have continued to move forward,” Holmes said. “It needs to rebuild its reputation for value and give customers a better, more reliable shopping experience. That takes sustained investment, which is made all the harder when you’re also managing a heavy debt burden.”

]]> 2474176Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Investors urge Foxtons to face up to property market slump https://www.cityam.com/investors-urge-foxtons-to-face-up-to-property-market-slump/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:06:34 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474133

The last couple of months have been littered with stories of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models going rogue, causing havoc and ignoring their human handlers; much like a superstar striker who refuses to sit in a 4-4-2 formation and park the bus.

Football is embracing technology. Computers and screens are being used to give or strike off goals; data is now firmly embedded in player analysis – in a move that has helped the likes of Brighton and Hove Albion and Hearts – and now Bundesliga side TSG 1899 Hoffenheim are using AI to help in their deadline day recruitment and matchday preparation.

The club take on Crystal Palace in south east London on Thursday, and their head of football intelligence Timo Gross says that their use of technology developed by German software firm SAP – the club’s front-of-shirt sponsor – is aiding them in spotting which weaknesses to target in the struggling Premier League side.

“We think about game preparation through a quicker search for clips, different patterns which are then used to really understand the opponent’s movements or patterns,” Gross tells City AM. “Especially for this game, the preparation is still running but it’s in the end phase so we’re ready to get this game running.”

While its main market continues to be the German top flight, SAP’s sport strategy lead Fadi Naoum says that the firm’s Sports One system has undisclosed customers in the Premier League and was used by some national teams at this year’s men’s World Cup. 

But is there a risk of the AI going solo and modelling itself based on rival data? Could one club use its systems as if it was its opponent and unlock an advantage? The answer is rather boring, if not reassuring, sadly.

“We are very strict when it comes to the GDPR, security and privacy,” Naoum says. “Why all the Bundesliga and our customers trust us is because we have for every club its own system – there is no cross-data, it’s up to the club what kind of data you feed the system.”

The growing use of technology in sport has some fans worried, and Gross admits that AI “will change the whole landscape of job profiles” at Hoffenheim and beyond. He talks through a scenario whereby the SAP technology is used during a transfer window to identify potential signings, injury replacements and to do last-minute reconnaissance on a player who has arrived into the transfer mix close to the deadline.

Patterns and behaviour

Their use of AI not only allows for the analysis of player patterns – shots, dribbles, chances taken and the like – but behaviours too. “You can think about body language, data points which weren’t there but now you have it as a side product,” Gross adds. But it won’t see human scouts replaced entirely.

“The data is then connected to an action to give actionable insight,” Gross, who joined Hoffenheim as an intern in 2013, says.

“This is where the validation process with a human being is also in place, but with the help of AI, everything is more efficient and more to a level that we have questions to ask which we didn’t before.”

It was inevitable that sport would eventually need to embrace the technologies that are going to power much of the world’s business sector across the next century.
