Before cloud computing became a boardroom imperative, founders were building it, server rack by server rack, cluster by cluster. And, of course, before fintech rewired retail banking, it appeared as a funding surge in deal flow data that most banks weren’t reading.

You see the pattern, and I’ve watched it repeat itself across several years of evaluating startups. The startup ecosystem is the world’s most underutilized business intelligence system.

Incumbents may amass wealth and power, but it’s the founders who choose to build. Which sectors attract a sudden surge of founding activity is a three-to-five-year leading indicator of where enterprise disruption is headed.

While AI agents garner the lion’s share of media attention and VC funding, deal flow suggests the next market for hypergrowth will be of the metallic persuasion. That is physical AI, which includes autonomous machines and smart manufacturing, among other sensor-laden systems.

Robotics and physical AI startups raised a record $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, or more than double the prior year, according to PitchBook. Genesis AI, which emerged from stealth with a $105 million seed round, recently demonstrated a wheeled robot that can bring physical AI into commercially relevant environments without needing to replicate the human body.

Physical AI: Intelligence inside

Physical AI systems can perceive environments, understand spatial context, make operational decisions, and act autonomously in real time across industrial and other settings. Physical AI systems move beyond static automation toward adaptive operations that continuously improve through interaction with the real world.

As with most tech trends, physical AI is driven by a coalescence of several technologies that have matured simultaneously. These include: multimodal sensing, edge computing, simulation environments, robotics foundation models, and world modeling systems. These technologies allow machines to collect information from the physical environment, interpret it in context, simulate outcomes before acting, and continuously refine performance through operational feedback loops.

In addition, the costs of several components that make physical AI possible have declined, with lidar, actuators, depth cameras, and sensors becoming more affordable.

For example, Waymo said its sixth-generation Driver system significantly reduced costs while increasing resolution, range, and compute power. The autonomous vehicle system used a suite of 13 cameras, four lidars, and six radars. Together, the technological maturation plus cost reduction cultivates the right conditions for physical AI to blossom.

Manufacturing, automotive, logistics, and healthcare sectors have emerged as major areas of capital concentration, with organizations actively piloting robotics to address labor costs and the scarcity of qualified personnel, and deploying them in harsh environments even as productivity needs grow.

Figure AI, whose humanoid robots assemble automobile parts in BMW factories, reached a $39 billion valuation within three years, the fastest path to unicorn status in robotics history. Investors are banking on general-purpose robot models doing for hardware what large-language models did for software. Why wouldn’t they? The deal flow is there.

Three stages of a disruption wave

Throughout the past few years of reading deal flow, I’ve identified a consistent three-stage pattern that plays out across every major technology disruption.

Stage 1: The founder surge

A new capability emerges, attracting a disproportionate number of high-quality founding teams. Capital concentrates. Failure rates soar even as the survivors are defining the category. As I alluded to earlier, generative AI shot to the stars in 2023. Agentic AI is now moving through this stage, while physical AI is just entering it.

Dyna Robotics, which is building foundation models that let one robot learn service tasks for hotels, restaurants, and laundromats, raised a $120 million Series A funding round within about a year of its founding.

Stage 2: The corporate adoption wall

Enterprises begin piloting the technology but struggle to move from experiment to production. The startups that survive stage one hit procurement cycles, integration complexity, and organizational resistance. We’re seeing this right now with organizations implementing GenAI and agentic AI tools without adapting their operating models, according to Deloitte.

Some organizations break through this wall. After recognizing that generative AI would fundamentally reshape customer service, Intercom canceled non-AI projects, reorganized product teams and committed $100 million to replatform the business around AI. That transformation produced its Fin agent which now resolves millions of customer service queries.

Another company, Maven Robotics, mixed palletizing in warehouses, and is crossing the wall one customer at a time.

Stage 3: Industrialization

A subset of companies cracks the deployment code. The technology becomes operational infrastructure. The window for competitive entry is closing. Cloud computing reached this stage around 2015. GenAI and agentic AI will land there within 18 to 24 months, as organizations redesign their processes and double down on their change management practices.

Kiva Systems‘ warehouse robots, bought by Amazon in 2012, grew into a fleet of more than 1 million. What was once a startup capability is now sophisticated infrastructure that new entrants can’t easily match.

The practical implication is straightforward: by the time a technology reaches Stage 3, the structural advantages of early deployers are largely locked in. The companies that used AWS in 2010 to save money eventually built strong engineering cultures, data architectures, and product velocity in the ensuing years.

Submit your innovation now!

Physical AI today, something else tomorrow

The same dynamic is playing out in AI today and the deal flow is telling us exactly which categories are where on that curve. For physical AI, the competitive advantage lies in the ability to build continuous operational learning loops where physical interaction generates data, data improves simulation and models, and improved models enhance real-world performance.

As the deployment of these intelligent systems scales, they compound advantages through infrastructure integration, operational feedback and real-world learning. More data, operationalized appropriately, yields better outcomes.

Most corporate leaders treat startup deal flow as noise. They may discount it as too early-stage, too speculative, or too distant from their operating reality.

But rather than watch startup deal flow to find your next vendor, watch it to understand where the next generation of your competitive environment is being built. Then calibrate your own development and strategic roadmap accordingly. The signals are there; you just need to know how to read them.

As robotics systems grow more capable — faster, more precise, and increasingly reliant on AI-driven vision and control — the humble interconnect is being asked to do more than ever. Signal integrity, mechanical durability, and board real estate are no longer secondary considerations in robotics design; they’re often the limiting factor. 3M has built out a portfolio of connectors, cables, and cable assemblies aimed squarely at these pressure points, and the company’s interconnect strategy for robotics offers a useful lens into where the industry’s hardware challenges are heading.

Flex Life Is the New Uptime Metric

Robotic joints, arms, and end effectors don’t sit still — they twist, bend, and cycle continuously, often for years without a maintenance window. Cabling that fatigues or fails under that mechanical stress is one of the more common causes of unplanned downtime in automated systems.

3M’s answer is a family of high-flex cable assemblies built specifically for motion-intensive applications. CoaXPress-compatible assemblies are flex-cycle tested to 45 million cycles, while USB3 Vision-compatible assemblies push that rating to 100 million cycles. On the flat-ribbon side — used widely for I/O and data runs in robotic subsystems — 3M offers a range spanning roughly 1 million to 100 million flex cycles, giving engineers a way to match cable durability to the actual duty cycle of a given axis or joint, rather than over- or under-engineering the harness.

For machine vision applications specifically, where camera cables are constantly routed through moving linkages, this kind of validated flex-life data lets designers make a real engineering trade-off instead of a guess.

IDC Termination: An Old Idea Still Solving New Problems

3M invented Insulation Displacement Contact (IDC) termination back in 1961, and it remains one of the more underappreciated tools in high-mix robotics manufacturing. Rather than crimping or soldering individual conductors, IDC connectors displace the wire insulation during a single mass-termination step; 3M IDC solutions can save up to 80% in wiring time compared with crimp-style connectors.

That speed advantage compounds in two directions that matter to robotics builders. On the production floor, IDC simplifies mass termination across ribbon cable and multi-conductor harnesses, which is particularly relevant given how much I/O and sensor wiring modern robots carry. In the field, many IDC-based connectors support one-hand mating and unmating, which shortens service windows when a module needs to be swapped on a production line that can’t afford extended downtime.

Board Space Is Getting More Expensive

As robotic controllers and sensor modules pack more compute and I/O into the same footprint, connector real estate has become a genuine design constraint. 3M’s response includes reduced-pitch options like the Cable Socket 451 and Header 452 Series, built at half the pitch of the industry-standard 0.100-inch grid — effectively doubling contact density in the same board area.

For lower pin-count applications — 2- to 4-wire sensor and signal connections that are ubiquitous in robotics — 3M’s Mini-Clamp connectors offer a compact footprint without requiring a full IDC harness, while the Mini Stack header and socket family pushes board footprint reduction even further for designs where every square millimeter counts.

Reliability Under Vibration and Noise

Constant motion brings constant vibration, and vibration is what turns a marginal connection into an intermittent fault. Several of 3M’s connector lines incorporate screw-lock retention specifically to maintain contact integrity in environments where mechanical disturbance is the norm rather than the exception.

EMI and crosstalk are the other reliability variable in dense robotic wiring, where high-speed data lines often run in close proximity to motor and power cabling. 3M offers cable and connector options selected specifically to help manage that interference, which matters increasingly as robots incorporate more real-time vision and sensor fusion.

For applications that need a sealed, one-piece solution rather than a discrete connector-and-cable assembly, 3M’s Molded-On Cable Assemblies provide a ruggedized, fully customizable option — useful where a robot’s environment (washdown, particulate, or extreme vibration) makes a traditional connector interface a liability.

Why This Matters for Robotics Engineers

Flex-tested cables, IDC termination, and reduced-pitch connectors represent the kinds of infrastructure decisions that can influence a robotics platform’s reliability and performance in the field. As robotic systems take on more autonomous, safety-critical, and continuously operating roles, the interconnects tying sensors to controllers to actuators become a real point of engineering leverage rather than an afterthought. 3M’s robotics-focused interconnect lineup, including high-flex cable assemblies, IDC connectors, reduced-pitch board connectors, and molded cable assemblies, gives design engineers a menu of validated options for addressing flex life, assembly time, board density, and long-term reliability. For teams building or specifying the next generation of robotic hardware, that combination of decades of interconnect experience and application-specific testing (like the 45- and 100-million-cycle flex ratings) is worth a closer look during the component selection phase, well before a design freeze locks those decisions in. Korean researchers have developed a beetle-like soft robot. Source: KAIST

When we hear the word “robot,” we still conjure up images of mechanical figures from old science fiction films. However, reality has long since evolved: We’re surrounded by smart vacuum cleaners, voice assistants, and even four-legged machines that mimic dogs. But what are these robotic animals?

They’re not just battery-powered toys. They’re complex electronic devices, infused with elements of artificial intelligence, that replicate the appearance and behavior of real or imaginary creatures.

These devices contain sensors, speakers, motors, and processor modules that analyze external signals. They’re controlled via mobile apps. Digital pets can make distinctive sounds, respond to signs of affection, answer to their names, and display a range of emotions—from delight to fear, from satisfaction to fatigue.

Manufacturers employ a variety of engineering approaches when creating these devices. Let’s look at some interesting examples.

Microrobot beetle and its relatives

A microrobot beetle might seem like a fun little gadget. But leading research centers such as the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) are working on developing similar insects (see image above).

So why are robot ants, robot beetles, and robot bees being created? The answer lies in solving practical and even humanitarian problems.

Cyborg cockroaches: Rescuers from under the ruins

In the spring of 2022, a tragedy occurred in the city of Changsha, China—a six-story building collapsed. Dozens of people were trapped under the rubble. Many remained missing for nearly six days.

Rescue efforts were hampered by piles of rubble and collapsed floors. Ultimately, 53 people died, and only 10 were rescued. In such operations, every minute is precious. Rescuers use thermal imaging cameras and comb through the rubble, but this takes precious time.

But what if cockroaches come to the rescue? These insects are fast and can penetrate even the tiniest cracks, allowing them to quickly survey the disaster area. But how can they be made to search for people? A team at Nanyang Technological University (NTU) in Singapore said it has found a solution by transforming a Madagascar cockroach into a cyborg.

A miniature backpack containing a microcomputer is attached to the insect’s back. It contains sensors that detect dangerous gas concentrations, as well as an infrared camera with a thermal imager, allowing it to detect bodies under the rubble. To prevent the insects from scattering randomly, but rather to remain confined to a specific area, the scientists have developed a remote control system.

Electrodes and a microchip are attached to the cockroach’s body. An electrical impulse to the right side causes the insect to move to the left, and vice versa. When both electrodes are activated, the cockroach accelerates and runs straight.

This cyborg can operate for long periods in rubble: the microcomputer is powered by solar panels. One individual can survey an area of up to 100 sq. m (1,076.3 sq. ft.). The operator controls the movement and monitors the signals from the sensors.

However, there’s a catch: to fully survey a large building, about 500 of these cockroaches are required, meaning 500 operators. And although the cyborg will indicate the location of the victim, it won’t be able to extract them—that’s a task for humans.

Robot ants: Strength in miniature

Stanford University engineers created mechanical ants capable of moving loads 2,000 times their own mass. For a human, this is the equivalent of moving a 150-ton whale.

Just four of these tiny animals can transport an adult, and a whole group can lift a concrete slab or rebar. This phenomenal lifting capacity was achieved thanks to a gecko-inspired paw design that provides a secure grip on any surface.

A special coating of microscopic rubber hairs creates a bio-stimulated adhesive effect: When the rope is taut, the robot adheres and releases when it is loosened.

However, this high performance requires a lot of energy. The battery can run out at critical moments, so in industrial settings, these ants are connected to a cable and used as towing vehicles.

Snake-like robot: Underwater repairman

Animal robots are capable of not only eliminating the consequences of disasters but also preventing them. Norwegian developers have created a 5 m (16.4 ft.) robotic snake for servicing underwater oil pipelines. It inspects pipelines, transmits images to a dispatcher, and, if a defect is detected, repairs it.

Equipped with manipulators at both ends, the snake can replace valves and clean deposits from pipes. These devices can operate at depths of up to 500 m (1,640.4 ft.) for up to six months, recharging at special stations.

Robot crab: Underground explorer

University of California, Berkeley, engineers developed a robotic crab for underground exploration. Using fabric scoops on its claws, it burrows into the ground, collects samples, and analyzes the soil. Equipped with sensors and a manipulator, it can determine the suitability of a site.

These robotic animals could be used in construction or agriculture, detecting pollution. In the future, such crabs are even planned for use on the Moon. Scientists are currently working on improving the design so that the robot can dig deeper.

More recently, open-source crab platforms are helping developers innovate locomotion.

Robot falcons: Airfield guardians

Mechanical falcons, developed at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, are already in service in Canada and Germany. They frighten real birds away from runways, preventing collisions that could lead to plane crashes.

Unlike acoustic cannons, which birds quickly become accustomed to, robotic predators exploit natural fear—they not only mimic predators but also pursue live birds, demonstrating dominance.

Robot bee: Space scout

A miniature robotic bee, the size of a pinhead, was created at Harvard University. Although it can theoretically pollinate plants, its true purpose is reconnaissance. Sensors mimic the vision and antennae of insects and transmit a three-dimensional image to the operator.

This micro-reconnaissance vehicle can fly, swim, and dive. It runs on solar batteries, consuming only 120 milliwatts—less than a light bulb. Scientists are confident that these bees will be useful for exploring Martian canals, lunar craters, and even the toxic clouds of Venus.

A variety of zoomorphic robots emerges

Today, numerous robots mimic the behavior of a wide variety of animals. Their advantage is the ability to move horizontally and vertically, navigate obstacles, and penetrate hard-to-reach places.

Unlike real animals or people, they do not require food or water, making them suitable assistants in deserts, mountains, and the exploration of other planets. They could be indispensable in rescue operations and scientific research.

For example, MIT scientists created Mini Cheetah—a platform used to test algorithms for guide robots and jumping machines. Chinese engineers have developed an insect-sized model that has the properties of spiders and cockroaches. Another robotic cheetah from DARPA reached speeds of up to 18 mph.

A flexible robot, modeled after the Caenorhabditis elegans roundworm, was capable of navigating around obstacles. Gecko Robotics has commercially deployed systems equipped with suction cups for vertical movement and can operate in hazardous environments.

Submit your innovation now!

Quadrupeds follow dogs as human companions

Some four-legged robots can travel over 30 km (18.6 mi.) without recharging and carry loads of up to 180 kg (396.8 lb.). They can transport the injured and recognize voice commands.

Three years ago, Moscow State University unveiled the first such robot in Eastern Europe, costing approximately 1.5 million rubles. The Unitree Robotics A1 model, weighing 15 kg (33 lb.), was controlled by powerful electric motors. It was even tested at a zoo to observe the animals’ reactions.

After testing, the design was modified, improving access to the internal subsystems. The robot is controlled by a joystick and connected to cameras and lidar for navigation. Its basic gait is a trot, and its speed is 3.5 km/h. The dog can change its gait, shake a paw, stand up, and lie down.

Unitree introduced the As2 companion earlier this year.

Animal-inspired robots evolve

Although today there are robotic kangaroos, insects, and reptiles, the dog was the first and most common prototype. This is due to the animal’s familiarity as a human assistant. The mechanics of canine movement (walking, running, jumping) proved optimal for engineering solutions. Robo-dogs range in size from a mastiff to a Labrador.

The predecessor is considered to be Phony Pony, a Californian robot from the late 1960s. It didn’t resemble an animal much, but it already had articulated supports, sensors, and motors, becoming the forerunner of all quadrupeds.

Companion animal robots offer therapy and care

Interacting with animals can reduces stress and anxiety. There’s even pet therapy. Pets are especially beneficial for the elderly with dementia, children with mental health issues, and hospital patients.

However, live animals require care, and they are often prohibited in medical facilities. That’s where companion robots come in.

New Zealand scientists have proven that interacting with them is just as beneficial as interacting with real animals. They are hypoallergenic, don’t require food or walking, and their behavior is predictable.

Joy for All

These realistic cats and dogs from Joy for All are covered in soft fur. Cats open their mouths, blink, groom themselves, and roll over when petted. Dogs bark in response to voices, respond to hugs, and their “heartbeat” changes. They fall asleep in the dark. Touch and light sensors are built into the body.

Scientists at Brown University worked on software to transform them into assistants for the elderly. The robotic animals can remind them to take their medications and find their glasses or keys.

Jenny by Tomobot

Tomobot has designed its realistic golden Labrador puppy for the elderly and children with autism. It does not walk to avoid creating a hazard. Jenny senses touch, responds to commands (called “voice”), wags its tail, whines, and snores in its sleep.

The robotic animal contains 50 sensors, 10 motors (seven in its face), and microphones. An app allows users to name the dog and update its settings.

PARO — a harp seal

This robot animal is listed in the Guinness Book of World Records as “the most therapeutic.” Developed in Japan, it promotes relaxation and positive emotions.

The seal pup is covered in sensory whiskers and tactile sensors, moves its paws, makes sounds, recognizes its name, and responds to affection. If ignored, it cries. The charger is shaped like a pacifier, and when removed, PARO makes a disgruntled squeak. Its personality changes depending on how it’s handled.

Aibo by Sony

This sophisticated puppy featured a camera, sensors, and 22 axes of motion. Its eyes are two OLED screens. Thanks to cloud technology, aibo remembered events, developed its personality, and learned.

This robotic dog could play, bark at strangers, patrol a route, and send photos to its owner, although this was primarily for entertainment purposes. Sony discontinued sales of Aibo in June of this year, demonstrating some of the challenges with developing robots for the consumer market.

Robotic animals could become part of our lives

Robot animals are increasingly becoming a part of our lives as therapists, assistants, and friends. They are purchased for children, the elderly, and people with allergies or restrictions on pets.

In Japan, where the problem of an aging population is particularly acute, these devices have long been part of the care system. Europe and the U.S. are also actively investigating them for hospitals and nursing homes, accelerating development. Electronic animals are not just toys, but an important tool for care and rescue.

A Section 232 investigation by the secretary of commerce found that robotics imports pose a threat to U.S. national security and economic competitiveness. Source: Office of the White House

Yesterday, U.S. President Donald J. Trump issued a proclamation stating that the secretary of commerce had submitted a Section 232 report about the national security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as related parts and components.

“Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors, see section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States,” stated the president.

“Robotics and industrial machinery are critical to virtually all modern manufacturing processes, including for defense, commercial, and dual-use purposes,” he noted. “Furthermore, robotics and industrial machinery generate substantial economic value and support important economic activities, including approximately $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024 and the production of approximately $86 billion worth of equipment in 2024.”

From mission-critical military and law-enforcement activities to critical infrastructure sectors such as agriculture, automotive, and electronics manufacturing, the U.S. government asserted that robots and related systems are vital to U.S. competitiveness. The value of such imported systems has grown over the past decade, and cybersecurity risks have also grown, according to the secretary of commerce.

The Section 232 statement specifically cited “advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles” as providing direct support to the U.S. military.

While investments in U.S. robotics production capacity have increased, they are not sufficient to meet U.S. demand, said the president. He directed the secretary and the U.S. trade representative to “to enter into negotiations with trading partners to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.”

Will this Section 232 determination lead to tariffs on foreign made robots? With most of the major industrial automation providers based overseas, it remains to be seen how trade negotiations will go. The threat of geopolitical rival China is motivating policies such as this investigation and recent FCC restrictions.

Submit your innovation now!

Experts expect Section 232 negotiations before any tariffs

Industry leaders and observers offered initial reactions:

“As I articulated last week on [a] panel at the Arrowfly RoboBusiness conference in Santa Clara with respect to the FCC action, this is another strong signal of government support for those working on developing and expanding domestic supply chains for robots,” Brendan Schulman, vice president of policy and government relations at Boston Dynamics, posted to LinkedIn.

He noted that the Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP) Robotics Commission reached similar findings.

“The next step for the federal government? Negotiations over the next six months with trading partners to adjust imports, and then further consideration of other trade policy measures,” added Schulman. “I am very pleased to see robotics gaining increasing attention and importance as one of the foundational technologies in need of broad, supportive policy action by the U.S. government. More to come, I’m sure!”

Robert Little, former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc., 2026 Joseph F. Engerlberger Robotics Award honoree, and business development advisor, concurred. “Robotics are critical for any country rebuilding its manufacturing. I’m thinking, what took so long to make this a priority?” he told The Robot Report.

“Today, we still have limited industrial robot manufacturing in the U.S.,” said Little. “Already, FANUC, Teradyne Robotics, and Yaskawa have announced investments aimed at expanding U.S. robot manufacturing. I expect more to come, and I hope this new proclamation helps accelerate it.”

“Yet, what concerns me most are the gaps in our domestic supply of components for robotics and industrial machines: sensors, actuators, precision gears, encoders and more,” he noted. “We need a much stronger U.S. supply base for these components. This is where we need the most help to strengthen America’s ability to manufacture.”

The Section 232 investigation does not mean that tariffs will be immediate, added Ash Sharma, vice president of research and chief information officer at Interact Analysis. “This shouldn’t be read as a new robotics tariff today, but it is a clear indication of the direction of travel,” he said.

“The U.S. government has explicitly identified its reliance on imported robotics and industrial machinery as a national security concern and is seeking to strengthen domestic production,” commented Sharma. “If tariffs, quotas or other trade measures follow, they could have meaningful implications for supplier competitiveness, pricing, and manufacturing localization in the U.S., potentially affecting not just finished robots, but [also] the components that go into them.”

The Robot Report is expecting more responses that will be shared in subsequent coverage.

]]> London-based AI startup Tallia, formerly known as Revax, has secured €4 million ($4.5 million) in Seed funding to expand its AI-powered research and drafting platform for tax and accountancy professionals.

The round was co-led by Outward VC and the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW), with participation from Portfolio Ventures, Expedite Capital, Paul Forster, Angus Miln and several angel investors.

“We are delighted to support co-founders Jack Mander and Alex Bartlam, building trusted AI systems for ambitious tax teams,” said Outward VC in a public statement.

The funding follows several European investments in AI-powered tax and accounting technology during 2026.

Germany’s mika raised €6 million to develop its AI-native accounting and tax platform, while Belgium’s Dytto secured €1.5 million for an AI assistant supporting accounting firms. Italy’s A-Cube attracted €4 million for digital tax compliance, and UK-based Zalos raised €3.1 million for AI-driven enterprise finance automation.

Together with Tallia, funding in this space during 2026 reached approximately €35.6 million in financing.

Founded in 2025 by school friends Jack Mander and Alexander Bartlam, Tallia combines experience in professional tax advisory with expertise in engineering and technology.

The founders established Tallia to address a challenge facing tax professionals: how to use generative AI to accelerate research and drafting without compromising the accuracy, traceability and professional judgement required when advising clients.

Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, Tallia has been designed around the requirements of tax practices, where answers must be supported by legislation, regulatory guidance and case law. Its platform uses a custom retrieval system to connect AI-generated responses with relevant tax authorities, helping advisers verify the information before incorporating it into client deliverables.

One of the platform’s central features is its ability to combine external tax knowledge with a firm’s internal expertise. By connecting to existing documents, contracts, templates and previous work, Tallia aims to enable advisers to produce research and drafts that reflect their organisation’s established practices and knowledge.

The technology also incorporates structured review workflows, allowing senior professionals to examine the reasoning and supporting evidence behind AI-generated work.

The platform supports workflows across Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, allowing tax professionals to incorporate AI-assisted research and drafting into familiar software. According to Tallia, its system can produce a fully cited first draft in an average of 30 seconds, while teams using the platform save an average of five hours per fee earner each week.

With its new funding, Tallia intends to expand adoption of its platform among tax and accountancy firms, helping professionals spend less time on repetitive research and initial drafting while retaining control over the advice delivered to clients.

]]> Europe’s startup ecosystem is often associated with major funding rounds, venture capital and ambitious expansion plans. However, some of the continent’s most interesting companies are taking a different approach, building their businesses without relying on external investors. From AI-powered software to sustainable mobility solutions, these startups are demonstrating that significant progress doesn’t always require significant venture capital.

Bootstrapping allows founders to retain greater control over their businesses, prioritise profitability and develop products around the needs of paying customers. While this approach comes with its own challenges, including limited resources and the pressure to generate revenue early, it can also encourage leaner operations and more sustainable growth.

Across Europe, entrepreneurs are applying this model to a wide range of industries, including legal technology, construction, customer service, sustainability and digital marketing. Their businesses highlight the diversity of opportunities available to founders willing to grow on their own terms.

With that in mind, we’ve put together a list of 10 promising bootstrapped startups in alphabetical order. All founded from 2021 onwards, these companies are developing practical solutions to everyday business challenges while carving out their own paths in increasingly competitive markets.

Chatarmin (Austria)

Founded in 2022 in Vienna, Chatarmin is helping eCommerce businesses improve how they communicate with customers through WhatsApp and AI-powered customer support. Its platform integrates with popular eCommerce tools such as Shopify, Klaviyo and Shopware, enabling brands, retailers and franchise businesses to manage customer interactions and marketing campaigns more effectively. Through automated messaging and personalised communication, the company aims to strengthen customer engagement and help businesses build lasting relationships.

Blulinc (Belgium)

Belgium’s Blulinc, established in 2021, is making electric vehicle charging more accessible and manageable for businesses. Its smart charging solutions help companies oversee their charging infrastructure, manage electricity consumption and simplify the administrative processes associated with electric vehicle fleets. By combining charging management with energy optimisation and billing capabilities, Blulinc is supporting businesses as they transition towards more sustainable mobility.

CENDAS (Germany)

Since its founding in 2021, Bochum-based CENDAS has been developing digital tools for construction sites, helping tradespeople and construction businesses manage projects more efficiently. Its software supports the entire construction process, from initial preparation and task allocation to project execution, documentation and progress monitoring. By connecting office-based planning with on-site activities, CENDAS aims to reduce administrative workloads and improve collaboration between construction teams.

Freda (Sweden)

Emerging from Stockholm’s technology ecosystem in 2025, Freda is developing an AI-powered platform designed to simplify legal and regulatory compliance for businesses. By automating complex processes and organising regulatory requirements, its technology aims to reduce the administrative burden associated with compliance and make it easier for companies to navigate changing regulations. Its approach brings AI-driven automation to an industry traditionally dependent on manual processes and extensive documentation.

Herodesk (Denmark)

Founded in 2023 and headquartered in Aarhus, Denmark, Herodesk is helping small and medium-sized businesses improve customer service through an AI-powered support platform. Its software brings customer conversations from different communication channels into a shared inbox, allowing teams to manage enquiries, collaborate on responses and provide more consistent support. By combining customer service management with AI-powered automation, Herodesk helps smaller businesses handle growing support demands without significantly expanding their teams.

Nimber (Portugal)

Portugal’s technology consulting landscape welcomed Nimber in 2022, when the Lisbon-based company was established to help businesses navigate increasingly complex digital challenges. Its services span technology recruitment, cybersecurity, quality assurance and AI-related consulting, supporting organisations that need experienced professionals and practical solutions for their digital projects. By combining specialist talent with technical consulting, Nimber aims to help businesses strengthen their digital capabilities and access expertise across emerging technologies.

North ESG (Denmark)

Copenhagen-based North ESG entered the sustainability technology space in 2024 with a mission to make ESG reporting more manageable for small and medium-sized businesses. Its AI-powered accounting platform helps companies collect, organise and document environmental, social and governance data, reducing the time and resources needed to prepare sustainability reports. Through automated workflows and AI-supported documentation, North ESG helps smaller businesses respond to evolving regulatory requirements and growing expectations around sustainability transparency.

Senja (United Kingdom)

Launched in London in 2022, Senja is helping businesses turn positive customer experiences into valuable marketing assets. Its platform simplifies the process of collecting, organising and displaying customer testimonials, allowing companies to showcase feedback across websites, landing pages, emails and other digital channels. With support for written and video testimonials, Senja makes it easier for creators, startups and growing businesses to build credibility and strengthen customer trust through authentic feedback.

Submagic (France)

France’s Submagic has been simplifying short-form video production since its launch in Paris in 2023. Its AI-powered editing platform helps content creators, marketers and businesses automate time-consuming elements of video production, including caption generation, editing and turning longer recordings into shorter clips designed for social media. By making professional-looking videos easier to create without advanced editing skills, Submagic is helping users produce engaging content more efficiently.

Vaskeladden (Norway)

Established in Oslo in 2022, Vaskeladden is bringing an AI-driven approach to Norway’s cleaning industry, using technology to improve how cleaning services are priced, sold and managed. Its platform connects customers with cleaning providers while automating important parts of the business, including customer acquisition, operational coordination and customer support. By centralising these processes, Vaskeladden is applying AI and automation to modernise traditional cleaning services and make everyday operations more efficient.

Building European startups on their own terms

These 10 startups demonstrate that Europe’s entrepreneurial landscape extends well beyond venture capital-backed technology companies. From digitalising construction and improving customer support to simplifying regulatory compliance and modernising traditional services, they are addressing challenges that businesses encounter every day.

Their different approaches also highlight an important aspect of bootstrapping: success is not necessarily defined by how much funding a company can attract. Developing a useful product, building lasting customer relationships and maintaining control over business decisions can be equally important measures of progress.

As Europe’s technology ecosystem continues to evolve in 2026, companies like these offer a reminder that ambitious ideas can take shape through different financing models. Whether they are building specialised SaaS products or applying AI to established industries, these startups show how founders can pursue growth while maintaining greater independence.

]]> Viridi, a British DeepTech that enables the transformation of waste carbon dioxide into chemical products, has closed a €2.6 million (£2.2 million) round to scale their technology, strengthen its team and support its expansion into Asia and the US.

The round was led by Odyssey Ventures, with co-investment from Alphatron Impact Ventures and follow-on commitments from existing angel investors. TOP Ventures, the corporate VC arm of Thaioil, came on board as a strategic investor.

This follows their €3.3 million Seed round in 2023.

Dr Daniel Stewart, CEO of Viridi, says: “Having a strategic partner like TOP Ventures look closely at our technology, see its value and choose to back it at this stage is strong validation of what we’ve built. We’ll be working closely with them to deliver our technology to market, starting in Asia. With Odyssey Ventures supporting our growth in the US, we now have partners who can help us take CO2-based surfactants to the world.”

Viridi’s raise comes amid a series of European investments in carbon utilisation and alternatives to fossil-derived industrial materials in 2026.

Belgium’s D-CRBN secured €17.5 million to convert industrial CO₂ into chemical building blocks, while Switzerland’s Seprify raised €13.4 million for cellulose-based ingredients.

In the UK, Uplift360 secured €7.4 million for composite regeneration, Sparxell raised €4.2 million for plant-based colourants and HexSeed received over €700,000 for CO₂-derived diamond coatings.

Alongside other comparable rounds, these investments and Viridi’s funding total more than €60.3 million, reflecting a defined sample rather than overall sector investment.

Vivat Wongnirund, Vice President-New S-Curve Business Development of Thaioil, adds: “We have followed Viridi’s development since 2024 and have been impressed by its progress, particularly in CO2-based surfactants. The technology has been tested in real manufacturing environments and shows strong potential for integration into existing industrial operations. Viridi’s approach to using captured CO2 as an alternative carbon input is highly innovative.

“This investment gives Thaioil exposure to an emerging technology that fits our future growth strategy in disinfectants and surfactants. We see this technology supporting the future development of surfactant production in Asia and beyond.”

A spinout of the School of Chemistry at the University of Southampton, ViridiCO2 was founded in 2020 and makes a special chemical ingredient (a catalyst) that helps factories turn recycled carbon dioxide (CO₂) pollution into useful materials for everyday products.

Normally, industries use petroleum or chemical processes that harm the environment to make the raw ingredients found in things like liquid detergents, cosmetics, glue, and mattress foams. ViridiCO2’s technology plugs right into existing factory equipment, allowing manufacturers to swap out those dirty fossil fuels for captured CO₂ waste without having to rebuild their facilities.

The technology is designed as a platform that can be applied across multiple classes of chemicals using existing manufacturing infrastructure.

Surfactants, key ingredients across home and personal care, are the first major application, with the potential to extend into other areas of chemical manufacturing, and, ultimately, remove fossil feedstocks from the supply chain entirely.

Ali Mitchell, Managing Partner, Odyssey Ventures, said: “Our commitment is to grow UK and European deep-tech companies that are solving some of the world’s most fundamental problems. Viridi is exactly that kind of company. Combined with a strategic investment from TOP Ventures, our support gives Viridi reach across both the US and Asia as it moves towards commercial deployment.”

Today’s investment builds on the launch of Vireya, Viridi’s first CO2-based anionic surfactant, in 2025 and the company’s Joint Development Agreement with Zschimmer & Schwarz, announced earlier this year, to accelerate the scale-up and market adoption of Viridi’s technology for sustainable surfactants.

]]> British VC firm Evertrue Capital, the debut fund of Yvonne Bajela, has closed at €15 million ($17 million) aiming to invest €299-€599k (£250k–£500k) at pre-Seed in founders building frontier technologies primarily in the UK and Europe.

The fund is backed by Phoenix Court through Basecamp, its fund of funds investing in a global community of emerging managers, alongside the British Business Bank, Better Society Capital, Bootstrap 4F (Invest in Women Taskforce) and Allocator One.

Yvonne Bajela, founder and General Partner at Evertrue Capital, says: “Over the past decade, I’ve backed founders who went on to build billion-dollar companies, and almost none of them looked obvious at the start. The ones I’m drawn to understand a problem deeply, often from lived experience, and have the conviction and discipline to build around it. They don’t always fit a familiar pattern, but their insight gives them an edge others can’t yet see.

“The best moment to invest is before the market has proof. That belief has shaped Evertrue. We make concentrated, early bets and give founders the capital, access and support to build companies of consequence.”

Evertrue’s close follows several European early-stage VC fund announcements in 2026.

In the UK, Nauta secured a €60 million first close to back software and DeepTech startups, while Project Ventures launched a €5.8 million fund targeting AI and research-led businesses.

Elsewhere, Germany’s Vanagon Ventures closed a €20 million debut fund, also backed by Allocator One, while Berlin-based solo GP Robin Capital just today also closed a €15 million second fund.

Spain’s Masia secured €18 million, Belgium’s solo-GP NewSchool VC closed €10 million, and Germany’s ZOHO.VC reached a €7 million first close.

These fund closes represent approximately €130 million in disclosed capital, rising to €145 million including Evertrue.

EU-Startups previously named Evertrue among the British Business Bank’s first microfund recipients in June 2026, having interviewed Bajela about her investment approach in 2021.

Zaki Gabe-Wilkinson, co-founder of YC-backed Revion, adds: “Yvonne was our first cheque and backed us from day zero. Her conviction in us as founders was clear from the start and she immediately got to work, helping us find top talent and opening doors across the UK and US to industry leaders and investors ahead of our Seed round.”

Evertrue was founded on a belief shaped by Yvonne’s career in investing: that insight often comes before the evidence. Yvonne was previously a Partner at Phoenix Court, home of LocalGlobe and Latitude.

After beginning her career at Goldman Sachs and founding her own company, she joined Mitsui & Co., where she became one of its youngest investment managers, investing globally in tech companies including Wise and helping portfolio companies expand into Asia. She later became a founding member and Principal at Impact X Capital, leading its Seed investment in Marshmallow, before joining Phoenix Court as a Partner, where she invested in and supported technology companies including Moove.

The post OPINION: Healthcare’s pilot culture is holding back HealthTech innovation appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Across Europe, HealthTech companies are developing new technologies that can improve patient care, ease pressure on clinicians and help health services make better use of limited resources. But while these technologies are often successful in getting into hospitals in the pilot phase, many struggle to move beyond that and secure long term adoption.

This is not a new problem. Companies working with large public healthcare organisations, like the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) or Ireland’s Health Service Executive (HSE), are familiar with the issues surrounding new technology implementation. These organisations work at a considerable scale with complex responsibilities and obligations around patient safety and public spending. In short, widespread implementation of new technology, no matter how innovative, can often be met with hesitancy. 

And while the caution is understandable, with so many companies unable to get out of the pilot phase, it raises the question of whether processes are designed to welcome innovation or whether they are designed to keep healthcare stuck in its ways. 

The problem with pilot culture

Pilots play an important role in healthcare innovation. They allow clinicians to assess whether a technology works in practice, from how patients respond to identifying changes needed before wider implementation. They are the first step to mass adoption of new technologies, but far too frequently, they are also the last step.

Wider adoption of successful pilots can run into issues on many fronts: Who owns the budget needed to buy the technology? Which team is responsible for implementation? How will the technology work with existing systems? Who provides training and support? 

These are all questions that should be obvious but are often addressed far too late and end up stopping adoption in its tracks.

Another issue is the fact that the clinicians who champion pilots are often the people most willing to experiment; some can even be evangelistic about new technologies. However, their colleagues may not have the same priorities or passions and so a technology that works well in one department can struggle to get buy-in from the key stakeholders across other departments.

Procurement can favour the familiar

Procurement is another point where promising HealthTech companies can encounter difficulties.

Healthcare procurement carries the huge responsibility of spending public money, meaning they need to find suppliers that are financially sound with products that must meet the appropriate clinical, technical, and regulatory requirements. They need to have complete confidence in what they’re choosing.

A young, unestablished HealthTech company may not garner that confidence, no matter how effective the solution they have developed is. Young companies are also up against it when it comes to meeting the requirements set out by procurement, which are often designed around suppliers with years of experience securing public-sector contracts.

This creates a difficult cycle where a company needs a contract to build its track record, but needs a track record to secure the contract.

Not to mention the fact that procurement’s decisions can often focus mainly on price, so a technology that carries a high immediate cost may struggle to secure approval.

The result of these issues can be an unintended preference for established suppliers, even when a smaller company has a better approach to a clinical problem.

When caution becomes culture

Similar to the case with procurement, healthcare providers have to make sure that what they are offering the public is backed by an incredibly high standard of evidence and accountability. This can create a culture that puts caution ahead of good clinical outcomes and this can actually create risks of its own, as delaying the adoption of useful technology as a result of being overly cautious can have negative consequences for patients, clinicians and public finances not to mention the commercial consequence for Europe.

HealthTech startups need to generate revenue, build a sustainable business and invest in further development. If the route from pilot to procurement remains unpredictable, companies may struggle to plan their growth or attract the investment required to expand. 

For many it may push them to look to markets where purchasing decisions are more straightforward, meaning healthcare organisations risk losing access to innovations developed close to home, while European companies lose opportunities to build global businesses from their early clinical successes.

Build the route to scale from day one

There are practical steps healthcare systems can take to improve the path from pilot to adoption.

First, the people responsible for implementation and procurement should be involved early. An enthusiastic clinician on-side is valuable, but a pilot also needs buy-in from finance, IT, operations, procurement and those who will support the technology after launch. They can’t be overlooked.

Second, pilots should be designed with scale in mind. Before a trial begins, the organisation and supplier should agree what success looks like, which outcomes will be measured and what evidence would justify wider deployment. They should also consider training, integration, support costs and the effect on existing workflows.

Third, procurement requirements should better balance risk, costs and the long-term benefits of proposed technology. And the evidence new healthcare companies are required to give should be proportionate to the contract and the potential consequences of failure. The size and the experience of the company should not determine the outcome if the solution they are offering is genuinely helpful to clinicians and/or patients.

Finally, healthcare organisations should learn from their own pilots. Sharing results, including unsuccessful projects and the reasons behind them, can reduce duplication and help other teams make better decisions when it comes to their own pilots. Working in silos doesn’t help anyone.

Innovation needs a destination

The NHS has previously recognised the importance of tackling the problems with pilot culture through innovation guidelines, which help innovators navigate the routes towards wider use.

In Ireland, the HSE’s Framework for Health Innovation was also introduced this year with the explicit aim of creating a more consistent pathway from local ideas and pilots to lasting impact across the health system.

These initiatives point towards the same underlying need: successful experiments must have a realistic route into everyday healthcare.

Europe has the talent and entrepreneurial ambition to build world-class HealthTech companies. Giving those companies a credible route from evidence to adoption will help ensure their innovations have the opportunity to make a meaningful difference.

“This funding will allow us to scale what we’ve proven on our first mission, Oasis Alpha: that microgravity can be a widely accessible industrial resource. We’re so excited to be able to bring this transformative capability to even more customers, and ultimately build a future where microgravity is used to make 10x better cures for cancer, 10x better semiconductors and 10x faster developed pharmaceuticals,” says Julian Rothenbuchner, Tumbleweed CEO and co-founder.

Tumbleweed’s funding follows a series of European SpaceTech financing announcements in 2026.

In Germany, ATMOS Space Cargo raised €25.7 million to develop orbital transport and re-entry services, while deltaVision secured €10.2 million to expand spacecraft component production.

Elsewhere, UK-based NewOrbit raised €16 million for its very-low-Earth-orbit satellite technology, and Switzerland’s Stellar Alpina secured €3.8 million for in-space propulsion systems.

In Austria, Vienna-based ENPULSION secured €22.5 million in March to expand its spacecraft propulsion business.

Together with Tumbleweed’s newly announced round, these financings amount to approximately €85.1 million.

“The fact that Austrian space technology is mobilising international private capital and is
already being used commercially in space sends an important signal about the strength of our research and business location. Companies like these strengthen domestic value creation, create skilled jobs, and demonstrate that Austria is internationally competitive in demanding future technologies,” adds Peter Hanke, Austrian Federal Minister for Innovation, Mobility and Infrastructure.

Founded in 2024, Tumbleweed sells modular payload containers (aka Pods) to labs, manufacturers and R&D teams. Pod is a modular payload container that handles power, data and certification.

The Pods are fault-isolated payload containers that arrive pre-certified and keep customer experiments powered and connected in orbit. Research groups, manufacturers and R&D teams send their payload directly to Tumbleweed, and receive data during flight. Pods come in different sizes, and mission costs start at €15k.

Oasis, their spacecraft, takes the Pods up, operates them, and brings them back to earth.

Compared to equivalent experiments conducted via the International Space Station, Tumbleweed customers reportedly ship 5x faster and 10x cheaper.

“Tumbleweed put Austria’s first commercial satellite in orbit in less time than it usually takes to certify a single experiment. Julian has done exactly what he told us he would do when we first met him, only faster. Now every lab and manufacturer can use space without becoming a space company first,” says Daniel Dippold, CEO of EWOR.

Oasis Alpha was built in nine months, five times faster than industry standard, and launched on 7 July 2026 aboard SpaceX Transporter-17 as Austria’s first commercial satellite, carrying four customers. The mission was sold out a year before launch and paid for upfront.

Today’s funding will fund three missions in 2027, carrying more than 10 customers. The capital will also accelerate development of Oasis Beta, Tumbleweed’s next-generation orbital platform scheduled for 2028, which will support larger payloads and feature re-entry capability to safely bring experimental samples back to Earth.

Robin Haak, Founder and General Partner at Robin Capital, says: “They call it a Solo GP, but nothing about building Robin Capital has ever been solo. Robin adds: “We want to build a home for exceptional founders, and stay with them long enough to help build exceptional companies.”

Its limited partner community includes entrepreneurs and families associated with businesses such as Ferrari, Moratti, Adyen and FTMO, alongside investors connected to Permira, Macquarie and FJ Labs.

These investment vehicles enable its investor community to participate in additional financing opportunities beyond the firm’s typical pre-Seed and Seed-stage investment strategy.

]]> Of the 12 companies listed by French AI unicorn Mistral as available Connectors (ready-made integrations connecting AI to external applications), not one hails from Europe; raising questions about the continent’s competitiveness.

Despite what this may imply, there are plenty of European software platforms that could potentially become managed Connectors for Mistral – many of which have even seen significant backing over the past five years.

Mistral’s Connectors allow users to link its AI tools with external services such as Gmail, Slack, Notion, GitHub and Stripe. Once connected, users can ask the AI assistant to retrieve information, analyse records and, where authorised, perform actions across those services without navigating between different applications.

Drawing on EU-Startups’ coverage between November 2021 and November 2026, here are 10 European startups and scale-ups whose products could plausibly join Mistral’s managed connector ecosystem.

The European Connectors

Attio (United Kingdom): Founded in London in 2019 by Nicolas Sharp and Alexander Christie, Attio raised €44 million in August 2025. The startup develops an AI-native customer relationship management (CRM) platform that helps businesses organise customer information, manage sales pipelines and automate workflows.

Attio is particularly suited to the connector concept because its software acts as a central repository for customer relationships. Its developer platform already supports a REST API, webhooks and OAuth authentication. A potential Mistral connector could allow sales teams to retrieve customer records, identify outstanding opportunities or update pipeline information through natural-language instructions.

Cloudsmith (United Kingdom): Belfast-based Cloudsmith raised €61.5 million in April 2026 in a Series C round. Founded in 2016 by Alan Carson and Lee Skillen, Cloudsmith provides a platform for managing, distributing and securing software packages and repositories. Its product allows engineering teams to control the software components used across development environments and monitor software supply chains. Unlike companies whose primary offering is integration middleware, Cloudsmith operates a standalone developer platform with its own customer accounts, records and management workflows.

Its REST API could support a future Mistral connector, particularly within Vibe Code. Developers could potentially inspect repositories, retrieve package information or review software supply-chain policies through AI-assisted workflows.

Factorial (Spain): Founded in Barcelona in 2016 by Jordi Romero, Bernat Farrero and Pau Ramon, Factorial raised €129 million in June 2026 in a Series D round. The financing valued the business management platform at €2.1 billion. Initially focused on human resources, Factorial has expanded into areas including expense management, project management and training. Its platform helps companies manage employee information, leave requests, administrative tasks and internal processes.

Factorial also offers an API and OAuth-based integrations. A potential Mistral connector could enable authorised managers to retrieve employee records, check outstanding leave requests or review administrative workflows. Its broad range of business functions makes it a credible candidate for extending Mistral’s capabilities beyond communications and project management.

Mews (Netherlands): Amsterdam-based Mews raised €255 million in January 2026 in a Series D round. Founded in 2012 by Richard Valtr and Matthijs Welle, the company develops a hospitality operating system covering reservations, hotel operations, guest management and payments. Mews also offers an Open API ecosystem, including a Connector API that allows third-party software to access hotel operational data.

While this API is not itself a Mistral-managed connector, it provides a possible route for integration. Hotel operators could potentially ask Mistral to retrieve booking information, examine occupancy records or identify operational tasks requiring attention.

Pennylane (France): Paris-based Pennylane secured €75 million in April 2025. Founded in 2020, with Arthur Waller among its co-founders, the company combines accounting, invoicing, expense management and financial reporting in one platform. Members of its founding team previously worked on PriceMatch, which was acquired by Booking.com in 2015. Pennylane provides APIs for accessing financial information and supports OAuth for integration partners. This makes it a potentially useful connector destination for Mistral, particularly for small and medium-sized businesses.

With appropriate permissions, an assistant could retrieve outstanding invoices, inspect accounting records or prepare summaries of company expenditure. However, because the platform handles sensitive financial information, any managed integration would need appropriate authentication and access controls.

Perk (Spain): Founded in Barcelona in 2015 by Avi Meir, Javier Suarez and Ron Levin, Perk secured €191 million in January 2025 in a Series E round. Rebranded as Perk in 2025, the platform allows companies to organise employee travel, bookings, invoices and spending. Its developer tools include REST APIs, webhooks and access to travel and expense data.

A potential Mistral connector could allow employees to retrieve travel itineraries, review bookings or request expenditure information without opening the travel management platform.

Personio (Germany): Munich-based Personio raised €190 million in June 2022 in an extension of its Series E financing. Founded in 2015 by Hanno Renner, Roman Schumacher, Arseniy Vershinin and Jonas Rieke, the company develops an HR software platform for SMBs. Personio provides tools for employee administration, recruitment, attendance, absences and other people-related workflows. Its developer platform supports third-party integrations through APIs with configurable access to employee and organisational information.

A managed Mistral connector could potentially help HR teams retrieve authorised employee records, inspect absence information or review administrative processes. However, integration design would be particularly important given the sensitivity of HR data and the permissions required to access it.

Spott (Belgium): Leuven-based Spott raised €18.3 million in September 2026 in a Series A round. Founded in 2024 by Lander Degreve, Manu Vanderveeren and Samuel Smeys, the company develops recruitment software combining applicant tracking, CRM and AI-powered workflows. The platform helps agencies organise candidate records, manage vacancies and coordinate recruitment activities. Spott also advertises an open API for custom integrations, alongside its separate MCP offering.

A potential featured Mistral connector could enable recruiters to search candidate databases, review recruitment pipelines or retrieve vacancy information through natural language. Its focus on a specific professional workflow makes it a particularly interesting candidate alongside broader business applications.

Storyblok (Austria): Linz-based Storyblok raised €73.6 million in June 2024 in a Series C round. Founded in 2017 by Dominik Angerer and Alexander Feiglstorfer, who previously worked together at a digital agency, the company offers a headless content management system that allows businesses to create and manage content across websites and digital channels. Storyblok has documented APIs for retrieving, creating and updating content, including OAuth-based access to its Management API.

A managed Mistral connector could potentially allow marketing teams to locate published material, prepare website updates or manage content without manually navigating the platform. This would give Mistral a practical connection to the publishing and content-management workflows used by businesses.

Typeform (Spain): Barcelona-based Typeform secured €123 million in March 2022. Founded in 2013 by Robert Muñoz and David Okuniev, the company develops online forms, surveys and interactive experiences for collecting information. Typeform’s documented APIs and OAuth authentication provide a technical basis for third-party integrations.

If Mistral introduced a managed Typeform connector, users could ask their AI assistant to summarise survey results, identify recurring customer complaints or create forms directly from a conversation. This would give Mistral access to a type of structured feedback data not currently represented by its featured connectors.

Leading this round was a natural fit for us, and we believe they are the team best positioned to set a new standard for how people build their careers,” adds Donatas Keras, Partner at Practica Capital.

Founded in 2025, Roleo is a personal AI career agent for technology professionals, designed to help people discover relevant opportunities and manage their careers without constantly having to search for their next job.

The company was founded by Janer Gorohhov, co-founder of identity verification unicorn Veriff, and Vahur Hansen, a former member of Wise’s early engineering team and co-founder of startup Membo.

Roleo learns about each user’s experience, ambitions, and preferences, identifies relevant opportunities across Europe, and connects professionals directly with employers when there is mutual interest – without the candidate submitting a job application.

Unlike traditional job boards, which require candidates to search and apply, Roleo builds an understanding of what each individual wants from their career. This includes not only their skills and previous roles, but also their expectations around compensation, flexibility, responsibilities, and future development. Users remain in control of their visibility, personal information, and whether they wish to pursue a particular opportunity.

Roleo’s user base already includes people from leading technology companies such as Google, Amazon, Stripe and Spotify. The service is free for professionals.

“AI is already changing how people handle everyday tasks, from managing information to organising their finances. Yet career management still requires people to do most of the work themselves,” Janer said.

“We want to build something that stays with you throughout your career, learns what matters to you, and helps you make better decisions over time. The goal isn’t to have AI make career decisions for people, but to make sure they have the right information and opportunities when those decisions matter.”

Since the beginning of 2026, Roleo’s agent has connected its users with 30,000 career opportunities they explored further.

Today’s funding will support both the company’s expansion across European markets and further product development, making Roleo increasingly responsive to individual needs and expanding the ways it can support users beyond job matching.

Markus Villig, angel investor, founder and CEO of Bolt, added: “I’ve watched Janer build Veriff and I know what Vahur did at Wise. Both know first-hand how hard it is to find and hire great people across Europe.”

Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas.

The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. Here are 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore.
