AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:50:30 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 US Air Force urged to move beyond KC-46 tankers as study backs blended-wing aircraft https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/usaf-blended-wing-body-kc46a-tanker-study/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:08:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55352 A new Hudson Institute study suggests the US Air Force reconsider its KC-46A strategy and invest in blended-wing-body tankers to double reach and save $15.5 billion.

The post US Air Force urged to move beyond KC-46 tankers as study backs blended-wing aircraft appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 7 min read
  • Hudson Institute study says medium blended-wing tankers could more than double effective refuelling reach compared with KC‑46A aircraft.
  • Researchers argue KC‑46 procurement alone will not meet future long-range aerial refuelling demands in contested environments.
  • Modelled fleet of 250 blended-wing tankers could save $15.5bn over 30 years while increasing fuel offload capacity.

The US Air Force should reconsider plans to continue buying Boeing KC-46A tankers and invest instead in a new generation of blended-wing-body aircraft capable of carrying more fuel over much greater distances, according to a new study that challenges the service’s long-term aerial refuelling strategy.

The Hudson Institute report argues that a medium-sized blended-wing-body (BWB) tanker could refuel more than twice as many groups of combat aircraft as the KC-46A, or support them at more than twice the distance. It also estimates that acquiring and operating 250 such aircraft could save $15.5 billion over 30 years compared with an equivalent fleet of KC-46As.

The findings come as the Air Force faces the costly task of replacing its ageing KC-135 Stratotankers while deciding whether to extend production of the KC-46A Pegasus.

Published on 27 October, the report, Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations, was written by Hudson Institute researchers Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin.

Their argument is straightforward: replacing old tankers with more aircraft of similar range may not solve the Air Force’s future refuelling problems.

“The medium-range KC-46A has performed well in contemporary operations and would play an important role in any conflict,” the researchers acknowledge.

But they conclude that the aircraft lacks the range, fuel delivery capacity and survivability needed to sustain large-scale operations across vast distances, particularly when tankers must operate from bases far from the aircraft they support.

The recommendation is an independent research proposal, not an official Air Force procurement opinion.

Why aircraft shape matters

A conventional tanker has a long cylindrical fuselage with wings attached. A blended-wing-body aircraft takes a different approach, merging the fuselage and wings into a broad, continuous lifting surface.

The shape reduces aerodynamic drag and improves efficiency, potentially allowing an aircraft to carry substantial fuel loads over longer distances without consuming as much fuel itself.

That distinction matters enormously in aerial refuelling.

A tanker must burn fuel to reach its assigned refuelling point, transfer fuel to other aircraft and retain enough to return safely to base. The farther it flies, the less fuel remains available to deliver.

The Hudson researchers found that this limitation becomes particularly severe when conventional tankers are required to support operations thousands of miles from their bases.

A purpose-built BWB tanker could change that calculation.

According to the study, the blended-wing-body tanker could deliver substantially more fuel than the KC-46A on long-distance missions. In some scenarios requiring large fuel transfers, the researchers calculated an advantage of up to five times.

That does not mean a BWB carries five times as much fuel in every situation. The advantage depends on mission distance and the amount of fuel required by receiving aircraft.

The researchers also examined the Airbus A330 MRTT+, but concluded that its somewhat greater range did not eliminate the same underlying limitations.

Fewer tankers could do more work

The report’s most striking findings concern how many aircraft would be needed to support a particular operation.

Using simulations of 32 mission scenarios across the Pacific, North America, Europe and the Middle East, the researchers compared the KC-46A, A330 MRTT+, medium BWB and two smaller tanker concepts designed to operate closer to potential threats.

Across the representative missions, the medium BWB required approximately 30% fewer aircraft than the KC-46A.

In one simulated deployment across the Pacific, moving an equivalent military force took 30 days using KC-46As but only 13 days with medium BWBs.

Another comparison examined the number of airfields capable of supporting sustained refuelling operations. Under one modelled scenario, the BWB could operate from 90 suitable airfields, compared with 31 for the KC-46A.

The difference is largely attributable to the BWB’s longer range, which would allow it to operate from more distant bases without relying heavily on other tankers.

That reliance is known as force extension. One tanker refuels another to increase the second aircraft’s reach. Although useful, the process consumes additional fuel and ties up aircraft that could otherwise support fighters, bombers or transport aircraft.

The researchers argue that a longer-range BWB could reduce this dependence and give commanders considerably more flexibility in choosing operating bases.

They also believe a dedicated refuelling aircraft could be cheaper to acquire and operate than a multi-role tanker such as the KC-46A, which is designed to transport passengers, cargo and aeromedical patients as well as fuel.

Those cost advantages remain estimates based on the researchers’ modelling rather than demonstrated performance from an operational BWB tanker.

JetZero offers a glimpse of what comes next

The Air Force has already taken steps to explore blended-wing-body technology.

In 2023, it awarded California-based aircraft developer JetZero a contract to build and test a full-scale BWB demonstrator in partnership with Northrop Grumman.

The aircraft is scheduled to make its first flight by the end of 2027.

Although JetZero’s demonstrator is not the specific tanker examined in the Hudson study, the programme could provide valuable evidence about the aerodynamic and manufacturing advantages of the configuration.

The Air Force’s interest reflects the potential applications of blended-wing technology beyond aerial refuelling, including military transport and commercial aviation.

JetZero is not alone in pursuing the concept.

Boeing, Airbus, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Natilus are among the manufacturers that have investigated blended-wing aircraft. Boeing’s earlier medium BWB concept provides the basis for the representative aircraft illustrated in the Hudson report.

The researchers note that improvements in aircraft design tools and composite manufacturing have made blended-wing configurations more economically practical than when the concept was first developed decades ago.

Commercial interest has also increased because of the potential to reduce fuel consumption and improve the economics of carrying passengers and freight.

A successful demonstrator, however, would be only one step towards an operational military tanker.

Such an aircraft would still need to accommodate aerial refuelling equipment, meet demanding reliability and maintenance requirements, and demonstrate that it can operate effectively from suitable military and civilian airfields.

Why the KC-46A is not being written off

The Hudson Institute is not calling for the immediate retirement of the KC-46A.

The Pegasus remains central to the Air Force’s tanker modernisation programme, and the report acknowledges its contribution to current operations.

Its concern is that continued purchases could eventually leave the service with a large fleet of aircraft that share the same fundamental range limitations.

The report notes that the Air Force plans to field at least 185 KC-46As, with the possibility of expanding the fleet to 260 or more through additional purchases.

It warns against allowing the convenience of continuing an established production programme to determine the composition of the future tanker fleet.

“A tanker fleet of KC-46As alone is insufficient to win in conflicts that require long-range, contested refueling operations,” the authors state.

Their alternative would involve reducing some planned KC-46A follow-on purchases and redirecting funding towards development of a medium BWB tanker.

One of the study’s proposed fleet plans, combining existing tanker procurement with the introduction of BWBs, was estimated to cost $15.5 billion less over 30 years than a plan relying exclusively on further KC-46A purchases. The researchers calculated that it would also provide 58% more fuel offload capacity.

The study argues that such a transition could be financed within projected annual funding levels, although developing an entirely new aircraft would introduce technical, financial and scheduling risks.

More than a question of buying new aircraft

The researchers also caution that even a more efficient tanker cannot solve every problem facing the Air Force.

Existing aircraft need better communications, situational awareness and defensive systems. Airfields require improved fuel storage, distribution facilities and protection against attack.

The study recommends that a future medium BWB be designed from the outset to accommodate advanced defensive equipment, potentially allowing it to operate somewhat closer to threats than conventional tankers.

This could reduce the distance fighters and other aircraft must travel to receive fuel, leaving more time and fuel available for their missions.

The proposed survivability advantages, however, depend on capabilities that have yet to be demonstrated on a full-scale BWB tanker.

The report also recognises a difficult procurement dilemma. Delaying the development of a new tanker would prolong dependence on the KC-135, some of which could approach 100 years of age before retirement under current projections.

Continuing to purchase KC-46As offers a more established route to replacing those aircraft, but could leave the Air Force facing the same operational constraints for decades.

The researchers believe the service should avoid making that trade-off by default.

Their findings do not establish that a blended-wing tanker is ready to replace the KC-46A. They do, however, present a case for developing one while the Air Force still has time to shape its future refuelling fleet.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • White House Halloween Air Force One flyover triggered air traffic disruption around Washington, drawing criticism over planning and notification.
  • Senator Tammy Duckworth demanded answers from the FAA and Pentagon over the low-altitude presidential aircraft flyover.
  • The flyover reignited debate over public communication and the operational impact of presidential events.

A low-altitude flyover by the US presidential aircraft during a White House Halloween celebration has disrupted air traffic around Washington, D.C., delayed more than 200 commercial flights and prompted criticism over safety, planning and the limited warning given to the public.

The incident took place on Thursday, 29 October, as President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump hosted a Halloween event for children at the White House. The presidential aircraft made two passes over the White House and nearby neighbourhoods.

More than 200 commercial flights delayed

As reported by Reuters, the flyover prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to temporarily halt air traffic at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), one of the capital’s main airports.

According to flight-tracking service FlightAware, 202 flights were delayed on Thursday, representing 26% of departures and 17% of arrivals. Most of the delays were attributed to the temporary disruption associated with the aircraft’s passes over the city. Some passengers reported that their aircraft were forced to circle before landing, while others experienced delays to their journeys.

🇺🇸 The new Air Force One THUNDERS over the White House right in the middle of the Halloween party 🎃 Not sure the kids expected a presidential flyover with their candy 😅 Writer: Lucas https://t.co/RCAJMFzxLR

— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 29, 2026

The disruption highlighted the operational challenges of coordinating presidential movements around one of the busiest and most tightly controlled airspace environments in the United States.

Limited warning raises questions

One of the main criticisms concerned the short notice provided before the flyover. The District of Columbia Council said residents, officials at the Pentagon and personnel at the airport received only around 15 minutes’ warning. Airline representatives also reported having less than an hour’s notice.

The unexpected appearance of a large aircraft flying unusually low over the capital startled some residents. Washington has extensive airspace restrictions, and the incident prompted concerns about the risks associated with low-altitude flights in a densely populated area.

The White House promoted the manoeuvre on social media, describing it as an “epic Air Force One flyover” for children attending the Halloween celebration. The FAA, meanwhile, said the flight had been coordinated with the agency and that a temporary ground stop had been implemented at the airport.

Senator demands answers

The controversy escalated on 2 November, when Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth called for a full explanation from the FAA, the Pentagon and the White House Office of Management and Budget. Duckworth, who serves on a Senate subcommittee overseeing aviation regulation, questioned the flight’s purpose, cost, authorisation and safety arrangements.

She also raised concerns about the aircraft’s reported altitude, with flight-tracking data indicating that it flew at approximately 400 to 1,000 feet during its passes over Washington.

Duckworth asked officials to clarify whether the flight had been approved for training purposes, what objectives it was intended to achieve and what minimum altitude had been authorised. The FAA and Pentagon said they would respond directly to her questions.

The White House defended the event, stating that the FAA had followed the necessary safety protocols. It also argued that the flyover brought excitement to children attending the celebration and to others who watched nearby.

A spectacle with wider consequences

The aircraft is known as Air Force One whenever the US president is aboard. Presidential flyovers have previously taken place at major sporting events attended by Trump, but the Halloween appearance has drawn scrutiny because of its impact on airport operations and the questions surrounding advance notification.

Beyond the immediate flight delays, the episode has raised broader questions about how ceremonial displays involving presidential aircraft should be planned, communicated and coordinated with civilian aviation authorities.

With Senator Duckworth seeking further details, attention is now turning to the explanations provided by government agencies and whether any changes to procedures will follow.

What began as a Halloween spectacle at the White House has therefore become a wider debate about aviation safety, public communication and the responsibilities that accompany presidential events.

]]> First look: Shield AI rolls out X-BAT 001 as autonomous fighter approaches flight testing https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/shield-ai-x-bat-001-roll-out/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:50:30 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55478 Shield AI has offered up a glimpse of its first aircraft, X-BAT 001, designed to fly without a pilot and controlled by AI.

The post First look: Shield AI rolls out X-BAT 001 as autonomous fighter approaches flight testing appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Shield AI has revealed X-BAT 001, believed to be its first flight-test vehicle, in a video showing the autonomous fighter’s airframe and markings.
  • Close-ups suggest its GE F110 propulsion hardware is installed, although Shield AI has yet to confirm the aircraft’s configuration and readiness.
  • Initial vertical takeoff and landing tests are targeted before the end of 2026, with production planned to begin in 2029.

Shield AI has offered a shadowy first look at X-BAT 001, believed to be the first flight-test vehicle for its autonomous, tail-sitting fighter aircraft.

A short video shows the aircraft inside a hangar, revealing its broad wings, digital camouflage and prominent engine exhaust. While the dramatic lighting conceals much of the detail, stills captured by Aerospace Global News offer a closer look at the aircraft taking shape.

AGN has asked Shield AI to confirm the vehicle’s status and configuration and is awaiting comment.

A closer look at X-BAT 001

The aircraft wears a grey digital camouflage scheme, broken up by dark edging and a contrasting central strip. “X-BAT 001” and “Powered by Hivemind” markings identify the vehicle and the autonomy software intended to fly it.

Its sharply swept wings blend into a substantial central body, with no cockpit or canopy. Panel boundaries and fasteners are visible in the closer views, alongside several upper-surface openings whose functions are not immediately clear.

Perhaps the most notable feature is the broad, mouth-like opening beneath the forward body. Appearing to form the aircraft’s intake, it gives the nose something of a whale shark’s profile.

Despite being designed to take off and land vertically from a tail-sitting position, X-BAT 001 is shown resting horizontally on ground supports. Shield AI has not explained that presentation. The footage does not show the aircraft being raised into its launch position or demonstrate its landing arrangement.

Shield AI X-BAT – everything you need to know about the AI-powered fighter jet Shield AI X-BAT – everything you need to know about the AI-powered fighter jet

X-BAT’s F110 engine appears to be installed

The video gives particular attention to the aircraft’s rear, including close-ups of a circular exhaust nozzle with overlapping metallic petals.

The assembly appears consistent with the GE F110 propulsion system selected for X-BAT. Its position suggests that propulsion hardware has been fitted to the airframe, although the footage alone cannot establish whether the complete engine installation is operational.

Shield AI’s chosen powerplant combines the F110-GE-129E with GE’s Axisymmetric Vectoring Exhaust Nozzle, or AVEN. The nozzle redirects engine thrust to provide the control needed for vertical flight.

In July, the companies announced successful integration, actuation and engine light-off testing at GE’s Peebles facility in Ohio. Those tests brought the engine, nozzle and controls together ahead of installation and flight testing on X-BAT.

The new footage shows no engine run or nozzle movement, but provides a much closer view of the hardware associated with the aircraft’s unusual takeoff and landing concept.

When will X-BAT fly?

Shield AI’s latest published schedule calls for flight testing to begin before the end of 2026. Its October update said flight-test aircraft were under construction and that weapons-bay aerodynamics had been evaluated in low- and high-speed wind-tunnel tests.

Speaking to Defense One in October, aircraft chief Armor Harris said two full-scale prototypes were being built, with initial flying focused on vertical takeoff and landing tests. He described an early operational capability around 2029 as the objective of a potential subsequent development phase.

Development flying will be based at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas. Shield AI has designated Des Moines, Washington, as X-BAT’s production location, with manufacturing planned to begin in 2029 and reach full rate in the early 2030s.

For now, X-BAT 001’s appearance offers a tangible glimpse of that ambition. The next milestone will be demonstrating that the aircraft can lift off, remain controlled in vertical flight and land safely.

The post British Airways resumes Dubai flights after eight-month suspension over Iran conflict appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • British Airways resumes Heathrow-Dubai flights, ending an eight-month suspension triggered by the Iran conflict and Gulf airspace disruption.
  • Daily Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner services restart, with British Airways planning twice-daily London Heathrow-Dubai flights from summer 2027.
  • Dubai route returns, but Middle East restrictions remain, as British Airways cautiously rebuilds services amid ongoing regional security concerns.

British Airways is resuming flights between London Heathrow and Dubai today (3 November), ending an eight-month suspension brought on by the outbreak of the Iran conflict in February.

According to Travel Weekly, the airline will operate the route using Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner aircraft, with one-way economy fares starting at £340.

Flights are scheduled to depart Heathrow at 20:00 and arrive in Dubai at 07:45 the following morning. The return service will leave Dubai at 10:00 and arrive in London at 14:55.

The first return flight BA105 is scheduled to depart London Heathrow for Dubai tonight at 20:05 GMT.

For now, the airline is restoring one daily service between Heathrow and Dubai International Airport (DXB). It plans to increase frequencies to twice daily during summer 2027.

The return marks a significant step in restoring British Airways’ Middle East network, although several other destinations remain suspended amid ongoing regional security concerns.

Why did British Airways suspend Dubai flights?

British Airways suspended its Dubai services along with services to other Middle East destinations following the outbreak of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran on 28 February 2026.

Military operations, retaliatory attacks and airspace restrictions caused widespread disruption across the Gulf, forcing international airlines to cancel flights or reroute aircraft. 

In its operational updates, British Airways confirmed on 3 March that it could not operate services from Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha, Bahrain, Amman and Tel Aviv. The airline extended those suspensions as the conflict continued.

On 16 March, BA cited continuing uncertainty and instability in regional airspace when announcing further reductions to its Middle East schedule.

During the disruption, the airline operated eight relief flights from Muscat, Oman, to help stranded passengers return to the UK. It also added flights between London and Singapore and Bangkok to accommodate affected travellers.

The Dubai suspension was repeatedly extended. Services were expected to resume on 1 July, but the airline postponed the restart to 25 October. At the time, The National reported that the suspension was continuing despite a pause in active hostilities between Iran and the United States.

Other British Airways Middle East routes remain suspended for now

Although Dubai services are returning, British Airways has not yet restored its full regional network.

According to TTG‘s 30 October update, Dubai flight resumptions will be followed by four weekly Amman services from 4 November. Riyadh services are scheduled to restart daily on 11 January 2027. Bahrain remains suspended until late March 2027 and Abu Dhabi until winter 2027–28.

British Airways’ return to Dubai is a positive sign for the embattled region, but international airlines will continue to assess operational risks before restarting their services. 

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) continues to warn of risks to civil aviation in the Persian Gulf. 

Under its latest conflict-zone guidance, revised on 30 September, airlines are advised to avoid airspace over Gulf waters within the UAE’s Emirates Flight Information Region, except where necessary for airport arrivals and departures.

EASA says these operations may proceed with appropriate risk mitigation and continuous monitoring. The agency continues to warn of missile and drone activity, air-defence operations and the possibility of rapid military escalation. The current guidance remains valid until 16 November.

]]> Bomb threats trigger security alerts on seven flights across four European countries https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/bomb-threats-seven-flights-europe/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:55:07 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55457 Flights from Heathrow and Manchester were among seven affected by bomb threats across Europe, triggering security searches and a temporary airport closure.

The post Bomb threats trigger security alerts on seven flights across four European countries appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Seven flights were affected by bomb threats across Poland, Spain, Italy and Bulgaria, including departures from Heathrow and Manchester.
  • A LOT flight diverted to Warsaw-Modlin, while other aircraft underwent security checks after landing at their destinations.
  • All aircraft landed safely and no explosives were found. Authorities have not established whether the incidents were connected.

Bomb threats on several flights in Europe today have seen aircraft searched and airports temporarily closed, with at least seven separate flights affected.

The incidents included a LOT Polish flight and a Ryanair flight, both from the UK; an SAS flight from Copenhagen; and at least two flights into Sofia, Bulgaria.

Separately, authorities searched two Ryanair flights upon landing in Rome Fiumicino, arriving from Dublin and Lisbon, following anonymous tips.

The incidents come one day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest after a mid-flight bomb threat.

All aircraft landed safely, with no explosives found in the searches completed so far. Each alert nevertheless prompted a full security response. Authorities have not established a connection between the incidents or whether it is a coordinated campaign.

Seven flights report bomb threats in one day

Two flights to Poland receive bomb threats

On the morning of 3 November, a LOT Polish flight departed London Heathrow for Warsaw just before 07:00. The Boeing 737 MAX, operating flight LOT286, was almost two hours into the journey when it received the bomb threat.

The flight immediately diverted, taking a sharp turn away from Warsaw’s main Chopin Airport and landing at the northern Warsaw-Modlin Airport instead.

Passengers were disembarked while security teams examined the aircraft. Modlin temporarily suspended operations while checks were carried out, but reopened a short while later.

BREAKING: Polish authorities are evacuating two passenger planes at two airports in the Warsaw area after bomb threats. One SAS flight from Copenhagen is being evacuated at Chopin Airport while a LOT flight is being evacuated at Modlin Airport. https://t.co/PXrgt9uCo0

— Visegrád 24 (@visegrad24) November 3, 2026

At almost the same time, an SAS flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw landed at its destination and was immediately evacuated, having also received a bomb threat.

SAS confirmed the incident, sharing, “We can confirm that a threat has been made against flight SK751 between Copenhagen and Warsaw. The aircraft landed normally in Warsaw and the passengers have disembarked.”

Three Ryanair flights searched on landing

In Spain, a Ryanair flight from Manchester landed in Murcia safely at around 10:30, having received a threat of a bomb on board.

All 114 passengers and seven crew members were disembarked away from the terminal while the aircraft was inspected by security teams. No explosives were found.

Two further Ryanair aircraft were searched at Rome Fiumicino following an anonymous warning alleging explosives aboard services arriving from Lisbon and Dublin. At least one of the flights was escorted by fighter jets, according to reports.

The Lisbon flight landed at approximately 09:40 local time, followed by the Dublin service at 10:44. Police and bomb disposal specialists checked the aircraft, passengers and baggage.

No explosives were found.

Sofia reports at least two bomb scares

Bulgaria has reported several affected flights, including a Wizz Air flight from Bergamo to Sofia and another flight travelling from Dublin. Seperate reports have claimed an EL AL flight from Israel had also declared an emergency due to a bomb threat.

The incidents at Sofia come just a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton was forced to make an emergency landing in Budapest after receiving a bomb threat mid-flight. The Airbus A321 was escorted by fighter jets before landing safely in Hungary.

Authorities there “carried out the necessary security checks on the aircraft and passengers”, a spokesperson for Wizz Air said.

The airline later confirmed an inspection had been “completed and nothing was found”.

This is a developing story and will be updated

In Brief 2 min read
  • Black Hawk helicopter narrowly avoided fireworks during a Seattle Seahawks flyover at Lumen Field before the NFL game against Chicago Bears.
  • Viral video shows fireworks exploding near a US Army UH-60 Black Hawk, raising stadium flyover safety concerns.
  • The military helicopter continued flying unharmed after the near-miss.

A US Army Black Hawk helicopter came dangerously close to fireworks launched during a pre-game flyover at Seattle’s Lumen Field, prompting fresh questions about safety procedures surrounding military aircraft appearances at major sporting events.

The incident occurred before the Seattle Seahawks hosted the Chicago Bears, with four Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters performing a pre-game flyover above the stadium.

What happened during the Black Hawk flyover?

Video footage shared on social media shows the helicopters approaching the venue in a diamond formation before passing over the stadium’s open roof. Three of the aircraft clear the venue before pyrotechnics begin firing.

However, the fourth helicopter remains directly over the stadium as blue and red fireworks erupt below, appearing to explode very close to the aircraft.

While some people sharing footage on social media thought the helicopter had been struck, other video shows the aircraft continuing its flight without any visible signs of damage.

The flyover was conducted by four UH-60M Black Hawks from the 2-158th Assault Helicopter Battalion.

Fireworks strike a U.S. Army UH-60M Black Hawk during the Seahawks–Chicago Bears pregame flyover at Lumen Field. https://t.co/0eA1Gyfapu

— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 3, 2026

What is the Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter?

The US Black Hawk family includes the S-70, UH-60, and SH-60 variants, of which there are around 3,960 units in service, mostly with the US Army.

The Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk is one of the US Army’s most widely used utility helicopters and has been in service since 1979.

Renewed questions about stadium flyovers

Helicopter flyovers have become a regular part of major sporting events in the United States, including NFL games at Seattle’s Lumen Field, which can host crowds of around 70,000 spectators.

The apparent near-miss comes just months after concerns were raised over another stadium flyover. In August, two Airlink Embraer E-Jets passed low over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium before a South Africa-New Zealand rugby international.

Flight-tracking data indicated the aircraft flew between approximately 41ft and 46ft above the stadium roofline as pyrotechnics were launched during the display. Airlink later said both aircraft operated within approved safety parameters and that the flyover had been carefully planned and rehearsed.

It is not currently known whether an investigation will be opened into the Seattle incident.

]]> What is aircraft overspeed? Understanding the condition reported before the Florida Learjet crash https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/what-is-aircraft-overspeed/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:49:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55437 A Learjet 60 crew reported an overspeed condition shortly before a fatal crash in Florida. What does aircraft overspeed mean and why is it dangerous?

The post What is aircraft overspeed? Understanding the condition reported before the Florida Learjet crash appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • NTSB says Learjet crew reported icing, turbulence, precipitation and an overspeed condition moments before the fatal descent.
  • Aircraft overspeed means exceeding certified speed limits, increasing aerodynamic loads but not automatically causing structural failure.
  • Investigators have not determined the crash cause or whether overspeed contributed to evidence of an in-flight breakup.

The crew of a Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on 1 November reported an overspeed condition shortly before the aircraft plunged to the ground, killing all nine people aboard.

During a preliminary briefing on 2 November, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said the pilots had encountered icing, turbulence and precipitation before the jet entered a rapid descent.

Investigators have also found evidence which suggests the aircraft may have begun breaking apart before impact. However, the NTSB has not determined what caused the crash or whether overspeed contributed to a structural failure.

What is aircraft overspeed and why is it dangerous?

Aircraft overspeed means flying faster than the aircraft’s certified maximum speed.

Aircraft have two main speed limits:

  • VMO: maximum indicated airspeed (at lower altitude) to protect the airframe from too much aerodynamic stress.
  • MMO: maximum Mach number (factor of the speed of sound) to avoid problematic airflow changes.

Overspeed is dangerous because higher speeds increase aerodynamic forces on the wings, tail, and control surfaces.

At lower altitudes, aircraft usually reach their VMO limit first. But the air is thinner at higher altitudes, so aircraft can reach their MMO limit before reaching VMO. Pilots must stay below whichever limit is reached first.

When an aircraft passes its speed limit, the cockpit may warn pilots with sounds and lights. An overspeed warning doesn’t always mean the aircraft will break apart. Planes are built to withstand stresses beyond certified limits, but going too far past those limits increases the risk of airframe damage and loss of control.

As an aircraft accelerates, the aerodynamic forces acting on its wings, tail and control surfaces increase. At a given air density, doubling the aircraft’s true airspeed produces four times the dynamic pressure, a major factor in aerodynamic loading.

Excessive speed can stress the airframe, especially when the aircraft encounters turbulence or during abrupt manoeuvres. 

At high altitude, approaching or exceeding an aircraft’s Mach limit can also produce shock waves that disturb airflow over the wings and affect stability. 

Overspeed increases risks of Mach tuck and flutter 

The FAA’s Advisory Circular 61-107B on high-altitude flight explains that changes in airflow at high Mach numbers can cause a nose-down pitch, which can impact aircraft control.

This dynamic, known as Mach tuck, can make recovery more difficult as the aircraft accelerates further during the descent.

Another potential hazard is flutter – aerodynamic forces can cause aircraft structures to oscillate. Severe flutter can damage or destroy components. 

Although exceeding operating speed limits does not automatically cause these dynamics, it does increase the risk.

What causes an aircraft to overspeed?

Overspeed can happen due to excessive acceleration during descent, turbulence, inappropriate power settings or difficulty controlling the aircraft.

A steep, uncontrolled descent is especially dangerous because the aircraft can accelerate rapidly as it loses altitude, even with reduced engine thrust.

Pilots attempting to recover must manage both airspeed and structural loads. Pulling back too sharply at excessive speed can place additional stress on the aircraft.

Overspeed can also result from an aircraft losing control, even if it is not the initial cause of an emergency.

Can icing and turbulence contribute?

Ice accumulation can reduce lift, increase drag and affect aircraft handling. Ice affecting sensors can also produce unreliable airspeed readings.

Turbulence can cause sudden changes in aircraft attitude, altitude and airspeed, making it harder to maintain a stable flight path.

At high altitude, jets also have a narrower margin between low-speed aerodynamic limitations and high-speed Mach limits.

These conditions can complicate recovery from an aircraft upset, although investigators have not yet established whether icing or turbulence contributed to the Florida crash.

What can pilots do during an overspeed?

Most modern jets have cockpit systems that warn pilots when they exceed operating speed limits. The appropriate response depends on the aircraft’s attitude, altitude and the nature of the emergency.

Pilots generally reduce thrust where appropriate and adjust the aircraft’s attitude to bring its speed back within operating limits. During an uncontrolled descent, however, regaining control of the flight path may take priority. Pilots must avoid abrupt control inputs because they can impose excessive structural loads.

What has the NTSB revealed about the Florida crash?

The Learjet 60 was travelling from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas when the emergency occurred.

According to the NTSB’s preliminary briefing, the aircraft was cruising at 35,000 feet when its crew reported light clear icing, moderate turbulence and altitude deviations of approximately 700 feet.

The pilots later encountered precipitation and requested clearance to climb to 37,000 feet. Less than 30 seconds after receiving clearance, the crew reported that the aircraft was descending and issued a mayday call.

At about 12:48 pm local time, one pilot transmitted: “We are in an overspeed condition. Descending.”

According to NTSB investigators, the crew reported descent rates that increased from about 10,000 to 22,000 feet per minute.

These figures describe its vertical descent rate, not its forward airspeed, and do not establish how far it exceeded its operating limits.

NTSB board member Tom Chapman also said investigators had found evidence of a possible in-flight breakup.

“We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact,” he said.

Investigators are examining wreckage, weather conditions, maintenance records and air traffic control communications to reconstruct the aircraft’s final moments.

The NTSB investigation, ERA27MA026, remains ongoing. The agency has not determined what caused the Learjet’s rapid descent or whether overspeed contributed to the apparent structural breakup.

]]> India’s $900m Boeing 767 tanker deal with Israel’s IAI moves closer https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/indias-900m-boeing-767-tanker-deal-iai/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:17:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55256 India is nearing a $900M deal with Israel's IAI to convert six Boeing 767s into refuelling tankers to replace its ageing Il-78 fleet.

The post India’s $900m Boeing 767 tanker deal with Israel’s IAI moves closer appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 6 min read
  • India nears $900m IAI deal for six Boeing 767 tankers, boosting Indian Air Force aerial refuelling capability and fleet modernisation.
  • Israel’s IAI is sole approved bidder; converted Boeing 767 MMTTs would replace India’s ageing Russian-built Il-78 tankers.
  • At least 30% of tanker conversion work could be completed in India with HAL involvement, supporting domestic aerospace industry.

India is moving closer to a $900 million agreement with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) to acquire six Boeing 767-based aerial refuelling aircraft, potentially ending years of unsuccessful attempts to replace the Indian Air Force’s ageing Russian-built tankers.

Israeli business newspaper Globes reported on 1 November that IAI was positioned to secure the contract after its proposal emerged as the only bid approved for further consideration in an Indian government tender. Another Israeli publication, Calcalist’s CTech, reported that the company was nearing an agreement to convert six former passenger aircraft into military tankers.

Neither report establishes that a contract has been signed, but it is learnt from the India Ministry of Defence that final details were being discussed with the Israeli firm.

The proposed acquisition would involve converting pre-owned Boeing 767 airliners into Multi-Mission Tanker Transport (MMTT) aircraft. india is expected to participate in the programme, with at least 30% of the work reportedly earmarked for Indian companies.

The first deliveries are being targeted for 2030, although the timetable remains dependent on a final contract and the subsequent conversion programme.

The latest reports follow an Aerospace Global News investigation published in October 2025, which revealed that India was preparing to acquire six converted Boeing 767 tankers from IAI as part of its long-delayed aerial refuelling modernisation programme.

At the time, a senior Indian Defence Ministry official told AGN that India’s existing relationship with IAI would make the transition and oversight process easier.

The agreement had then been expected before the end of March 2026. That deadline passed without a publicly confirmed contract, underscoring the delays surrounding the procurement.

Why India urgently needs new refuelling aircraft

The Indian Air Force currently relies on six Ilyushin Il-78MKI tankers acquired from Russia in 2003–04.

Based at Agra in northern India, the aircraft have provided India’s principal air-to-air refuelling capability for more than two decades. They allow fighters such as the Rafale and Su-30MKI to remain airborne longer, undertake extended missions and operate farther from their home bases.

Aerial refuelling is particularly important for India because of the distances involved in operations over the Himalayas and the Indian Ocean.

A fighter’s operational reach is limited by the fuel it can carry. Tanker support allows it to replenish fuel during flight instead of returning to an airbase, increasing the time available for patrols, interceptions and strike missions.

However, the Il-78 fleet has suffered persistent serviceability problems.

As AGN reported in October 2025, an audit by India’s Comptroller and Auditor General identified several shortcomings affecting the fleet, including unreliable refuelling pods, maintenance difficulties, inadequate infrastructure and restrictions associated with operating the heavy aircraft from certain runways.

The small fleet has also faced availability problems, leaving the IAF with limited capacity when aircraft are undergoing maintenance.

India has consequently turned to leased aerial refuelling services as an interim measure while pursuing a permanent replacement.

The acquisition of six new tankers would provide a modern replacement capability, although the IAF’s wider refuelling requirements could eventually demand a larger fleet.

Boeing 767 conversion offers an alternative to new-build tankers

The proposed aircraft would be based on Boeing 767 passenger jets acquired from the commercial market and modified for military use.

IAI’s aviation division has extensive experience converting commercial aircraft, including Boeing 767s, for specialised missions.

The tanker version would be equipped with systems to transfer fuel to other aircraft in flight. IAI’s MMTT design can accommodate both a refuelling boom and hose-and-drogue equipment, allowing it to support different types of receiving aircraft.

This flexibility matters to the IAF, whose combat fleet includes aircraft of Russian, French and Indian origin.

Aerial refuelling is not the aircraft’s only intended role. The MMTT concept also allows passenger and cargo transport configurations, giving the air force additional flexibility when tankers are not required for refuelling missions.

Using second-hand airliners is expected to reduce acquisition costs compared with buying newly manufactured military tankers. However, the aircraft would still require substantial structural work, installation of specialised systems, testing and military certification before entering service.

The Boeing 767 option is separate from Boeing’s new-build KC-46A tanker, which is also based on the 767 airframe.

HAL partnership could bring conversion work to India

The proposed arrangement builds on a partnership announced in April 2022, when IAI and HAL signed a memorandum of understanding to undertake Multi-Mission Tanker Transport conversions in India.

Under the agreement, HAL was expected to convert pre-owned aircraft for aerial refuelling and transport missions, while also undertaking aircraft life-extension work and maintenance in India. The agreement covered commercial passenger-to-freighter conversions as well.

Announcing the partnership at the time, then HAL Chairman and Managing Director R. Madhavan described the tanker conversion business as “one of the strategic diversification avenue identified by HAL.”

The then CEO of IAI Boaz Levy said the partnership would bring tanker conversion work to India by drawing on HAL’s manufacturing capabilities, workforce and domestic supply chain.

The 2022 agreement did not constitute an order from the Indian Air Force. However, it established the industrial framework for the Boeing 767 conversion proposal now reportedly approaching a procurement decision.

Indian industrial participation is a significant element of the proposed agreement.

According to the Israeli reports, at least 30% of the conversion work would be carried out in India

The arrangement would involve technology transfer and participation in aircraft modification, although the precise division of work between IAI and HAL has not been officially disclosed.

IAI and HAL already have an established relationship in India’s defence aviation sector. The Israeli company has also worked with Indian organisations on radar, missile and other military systems.

One of the largest joint programmes has been the Barak 8 medium-range surface-to-air missile system, developed through cooperation between IAI and India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation.

The tanker programme could extend that relationship into the conversion and support of large military aircraft.

IAI also has a substantial commercial aircraft conversion business, including Boeing 767 passenger-to-freighter modifications. That experience provides an industrial foundation for the proposed tanker work, although a military refuelling conversion requires different equipment and certification.

India has struggled to buy tankers for years

India’s effort to expand its aerial refuelling fleet has repeatedly encountered delays.

Earlier competitions involving the Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport failed to result in a purchase, with acquisition costs among the major obstacles.

The IAF has subsequently examined alternative approaches, including converting commercial aircraft and leasing refuelling capacity.

In December 2025, reports indicated that India was considering a wider requirement involving 12 aircraft, potentially divided between six converted tankers and six new-build aircraft.

The reported IAI agreement concerns the six-aircraft conversion proposal. It does not establish whether India has abandoned or retained the possibility of a separate new-build tanker acquisition.

The Airbus A330 MRTT and Boeing KC-46A have featured in discussions surrounding India’s broader tanker requirements.

The attraction of the converted Boeing 767 lies partly in the prospect of obtaining a capable aircraft at a lower purchase price while involving Indian industry in the programme.

However, the first aircraft would not arrive immediately. The reported 2030 delivery target means the IAF will have to continue relying on its existing Il-78 fleet and interim refuelling arrangements for several more years.

The latest reports suggest that IAI is closer to securing the contract than at any previous stage of the procurement. The decisive step remains an official selection and a signed agreement.

]]> IndiGo confirms lie-flat business class on Airbus A350s as it targets long-haul market https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/indigo-airbus-a350-lie-flat-business-class/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:31:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55344 IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh said the airline will offer lie-flat business class seats and premium economy cabins on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft.

The post IndiGo confirms lie-flat business class on Airbus A350s as it targets long-haul market appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • IndiGo will introduce lie-flat business class, premium economy and economy cabins on its first 10 Airbus A350-900s from 2028.
  • CEO Willie Walsh said lie-flat seats are essential to compete for premium passengers on long-haul international routes.
  • IndiGo plans to expand premium seating across future A350s and potentially Airbus A321XLRs as its network grows.

IndiGo will introduce lie-flat business class seats and premium economy cabins on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft when deliveries begin in the second quarter of 2028, as India’s largest airline prepares to expand its long-haul international network.

CEO Willie Walsh confirmed the cabin plans during a press briefing in New Delhi on Monday, 2 November, saying IndiGo intends to compete for premium passengers while maintaining its low-fare business model.

The first ten A350-900s will feature three cabin classes, including 16 lie-flat business class seats, premium economy and economy. IndiGo has 60 A350s on order, and the cabin configuration for the first ten aircraft is already set. Walsh said later aircraft could introduce a larger business class cabin footprint with more lie-flat seats.

“I personally believe there’s a strong case for that (lie-flat seats in business class) given how we’ve seen premium demand strengthen right across the world,” he told reporters, according to The Indian Express. “It was also clear to us that to serve the long-haul international market, we needed to have flatbeds as part of the business class product. That’s what the customer expects today.”

IndiGo considers lie-flat seats for future A321XLR deliveries

The premium cabin strategy could extend beyond IndiGo’s widebody fleet. Walsh said future Airbus A321XLR deliveries would also feature lie-flat business-class seats, allowing the airline to offer a more competitive product on longer narrowbody routes.

IndiGo currently operates A321XLR aircraft with its existing IndiGoStretch product, which uses reclining seats.

The A321XLR is an important part of IndiGo’s international expansion, allowing the carrier to operate longer routes with fewer seats than a widebody aircraft.

The airline has already deployed the type on European services, including Mumbai–Amsterdam. IndiGo transferred the route from a damp-leased Boeing 787-9 after ending its widebody leasing arrangement with Norse Atlantic Airways in October.

In its 31 July announcement, IndiGo confirmed that it would suspend its London Heathrow services until its new A350-900 aircraft arrived.

Walsh told reporters at Monday’s press conference that IndiGo would maintain A321XLR operations to Amsterdam to retain valuable airport slots ahead of the A350’s introduction, Bloomberg reported.

A low-cost airline moves further into premium travel

The A350 cabin plans represent another step in IndiGo’s move beyond its traditional single-class, low-fare operating model.

The airline introduced IndiGoStretch on selected domestic routes before expanding its premium offering as part of its broader international strategy. Introducing premium economy and lie-flat business class on the A350s will put IndiGo in more direct competition with full-service international airlines, including Air India, on long-haul routes.

This hybrid low-cost premium approach has precedents. Thai AirAsia X offers lie-flat seating on its long-haul Airbus A330-300s. 

JetBlue has proven the commercial potential of private, lie-flat business-class suites on single-aisle aircraft. Its Airbus A321LRs offer 24 Mint suites on transatlantic routes, while its A321neos offer 16 Mint suites. JetBlue also offers a Mint cabin on selected transcontinental services, including routes connecting New York and Boston with West Coast destinations, as well as selected Caribbean and Latin American services.  

Both carriers compete for premium passengers while keeping their low-fare model. 

Walsh emphasised that IndiGo does not intend to abandon its cost discipline. Maintaining a competitive cost base is central to IndiGo’s strategy, even as it invests in new aircraft, longer routes and higher-value cabin products.

The A350-900s will give IndiGo the range to serve destinations deeper into Europe and potentially North America, complementing the A321XLR’s role on medium- and longer-haul routes.

The airline has not yet confirmed the seat manufacturer, detailed cabin layout or onboard amenities for its A350 fleet.

With the first ten aircraft confirmed to offer 16 lie-flat seats, attention will now turn to how IndiGo will increase the share of premium seats on later aircraft deliveries as it builds its long-haul network.

]]> NTSB to review Learjet 60 history during Florida crash investigation https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ntsb-learjet-60-investigation/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:02:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55368 NTSB investigators say they will review both the aircraft type and the specific aircraft involved as part of the ongoing Florida crash investigation.

The post NTSB to review Learjet 60 history during Florida crash investigation appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 2 min read
  • NTSB reviewing Learjet 60 operational history as part of Florida crash investigation, but says no similar accident trend identified.
  • Board member Tom Chapman said investigators are not currently aware of a history of this accident type.
  • Investigation remains ongoing, with NTSB examining wreckage, weather and maintenance records; no cause has yet been determined.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will examine the operational history of the Learjet 60 as part of its investigation into the fatal crash in Florida on 1 November.

Speaking during a media briefing on Tuesday, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said investigators would review both the model’s historical record and the history of the specific aircraft involved in the accident.

“I don’t believe we have any indication that there’s a history of this type of accident with this model of aircraft,” Chapman said.

“We’ll certainly look for trends not only with this model of aircraft – I’m not aware of any right now – but also with this specific aircraft too, whether there’s any history.”

The comments come as investigators continue to analyse wreckage, weather data, maintenance records and other evidence from the crash. No cause has yet been determined.

What is known about the Learjet 60’s operating history?

The Learjet 60 entered service in the early 1990s and has been widely used in corporate, charter and private aviation.

As with many aircraft types that have operated for decades, the Learjet 60 has been involved in a number of accidents and incidents during its service life. However, those events occurred in different circumstances and investigations have identified a range of contributing factors.

Learjet 60 crash: What is a horizontal stabiliser, and why is it essential to flight? Learjet 60 crash: What is a horizontal stabiliser, and why is it essential to flight?

2008 Columbia accident

One of the most significant accidents involving the type occurred in September 2008, when a Learjet 60 overran the runway during a rejected take-off at Columbia Metropolitan Airport in South Carolina. Four people were killed.

The NTSB found that the accident involved a combination of tyre maintenance issues, pilot actions and aircraft-system factors, and issued a number of safety recommendations following the investigation.

Other accidents involving the Learjet 60 have included runway overruns and approach-and-landing incidents, but they have not necessarily involved the same causes or circumstances.

What are investigators looking at after the Florida crash?

At present, investigators have not identified any connection between the Florida incident and previous Learjet 60 accidents.

The review forms part of the NTSB’s wider investigation into the accident, which remains ongoing.

For now, the agency says it has no indication that the Florida accident forms part of a known pattern involving the Learjet 60.

}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {

 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */

 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}

 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}

.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;
 margin: 32px 0 40px;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-field-intro-block{margin: 0 0 48px;}
.sie-field-intro-block p{font-size: 17px;
 line-height: 1.78;
 color: #374151;
 margin: 0;

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
	<li><a class="external-link eac-external-link" href="https://twitter.com/search?q=%23TheFutureIsYours" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">#TheFutureIsYours</a></li>

</ul>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>

                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
